+## Why it matters: the business case
+
+Large buyers often pay their suppliers' invoices weeks or months after delivery. A
+supplier that needs the cash sooner can draw it from a bank against those invoices,
+and repay when the buyer pays. That is receivables finance, and its numbers are
+sensitive in a specific way:
+
+- **A supplier's drawings show its cash position.** One that draws more, or more
+  often, is short of cash. Published, that tells its competitors, its customers and
+  its other lenders.
+- **The bank's limits and balances are its book.** What it has lent each supplier,
+  and against what limit, is its exposure, and it does not publish that.
+- **The suppliers should not see each other.** A supplier that could read another's
+  limit and drawings would learn its position and what the bank granted it.
+
+Why put this on a shared ledger at all? Off one, the same facility lives in several
+records, the bank's and each supplier's, which have to be reconciled. The usual case for a
+shared ledger is one record that the bank, the suppliers and a supervisor all read,
+with the money moving on that record. This post does not test that case. It tests
+whether the privacy the business needs survives the move.
+
+That is the dilemma. On a public ledger in plaintext, every drawing is published, and
+with it each supplier's cash position. On a private ledger, much of what a shared
+record was for is given up. Confidential transfers are an attempt at the middle:
+amounts encrypted on a public ledger, and readable by the parties who answer for the
+book.
+
+So a business would ask concrete questions before using them:
+
+1. Can the public see what each supplier draws and owes?
+2. Can the public see who draws, and when?
+3. Can one supplier see another's position?
+4. Can the bank see every position? It lends the money, so it must.
+5. Can an auditor or supervisor see them too?
+6. What happens if someone loses a key?
+7. What can the bank do to a supplier's balance without the supplier?
+
+The facility below answers them as it ran on Devnet.
+
+---

+**Against the business case's questions:**
+
+1. **What each supplier draws and owes:** hidden from the public, though the public
+   totals bound it.
+2. **Who draws, and when:** public (P-11). A supplier that moves from monthly to
+   weekly drawings shows as short of cash without one amount being known. One
+   proposed remedy, the float sending to every supplier on a fixed schedule whether
+   or not money moves, has not been shown to work, so I do not offer it as one
+   (B-10).
+3. **One supplier, another's position:** hidden from it, as from the public. Each
+   holder's key decrypts its own balance (E-52).
+4. **The bank:** reads every position, always (P-9).
+5. **An auditor:** reads every position too, if the token names one, and only one
+   is supported (E-11). That is a statement about who can decrypt what, not a claim
+   that it meets any regulator's requirements (P-6).
+6. **A lost key:** if a supplier loses its key and any seed it could be re-derived
+   from, the balance cannot be spent. The only remedy is a clawback, if the token
+   allows one, and it destroys the balance (P-10, E-12).
+7. **The bank, as issuer:** it cannot spend a supplier's balance. If the token's
+   settings allow, it can destroy one or freeze one (E-12, E-290).
+
+So the business case holds for amounts and fails for relationships. A supplier that
+minds being seen to borrow at all, or how often, gets no cover from XLS-96.
+
 Two limits of that run. First, it read the ledger through a public Devnet node. The
 design requires a node on the same machine, and a local Devnet node never finished
 syncing on the hardware I had, so I accepted that as a named risk (E-148, E-151).

 # Nostr (single note)
 
-Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on its Devnet, under a standard called XLS-96. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it to find out exactly what it hides. The short answer: amounts, not relationships.
+Confidential transfers on the XRP Ledger, XLS-96, are confidentiality from the public, not from the issuer. I ran them on Devnet with a small invoice-finance example to find exactly what they hide: amounts, not relationships.
 
 Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each transfer between confidential balances.
 
 Public: who pays whom, when and how often; every amount moved into or out of confidential form; and some zero balances, which anyone can recompute from public inputs. I matched that fixed encryption of zero byte for byte against live Devnet state.
 
-It is confidentiality from the public, not from the issuer. The token's issuer reads every balance, always, and no setting turns that off. If the token allows clawback, the issuer can destroy a confidential balance, and unless the token's flags were fixed when it was created, it can turn on locking later and freeze one.
+The token's issuer reads every balance, always, and no setting turns that off. If the token allows clawback, the issuer can destroy a confidential balance, and unless the token's flags were fixed when it was created, it can turn on locking later and freeze one.
 
-Keys are for life: no rotation or recovery in XLS-96, or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.
+Keys cannot be rotated or recovered, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet. A draft standard, XLS-99, would add both; those three networks do not know it yet.
 
-I started the same study on EVM chains at the same time. Those results will follow.
+I am running the same study on EVM chains. Those results will follow.
 
 A research project on Devnet, not audited and not production-ready. Eleven issues went upstream; five are resolved so far.
 
 Write-up: https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
 Code: https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions
 
-#XRPL #privacy #zeroknowledge
+#XRPL #privacy

The bank, which issues the token and reads every balance, funds the Dedicated Account with a public payment. The Dedicated Account makes one Convert of the whole float, amount public, so the float is confidential. Drawdowns and repayments are Sends between the float and suppliers A, B and C: amounts hidden, who and when public; each supplier's limit, draws and what it owes are hidden. +## What to take from it
+
+- **XLS-96 hides amounts, not relationships.** Balances and Send amounts are
+  hidden from the public. Who pays whom, when and how often is not.
+- **The edges are public.** Every Convert and ConvertBack publishes its amount, and
+  the totals bound what is hidden.
+- **The issuer sees everything.** It reads every balance, can destroy one by
+  clawback, and may be able to freeze one.
+- **Keys are for life.** No rotation and no recovery, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet,
+  Testnet or Devnet today. XLS-99 is a draft that would add both.
+- **Running it found things reading did not**, and reading what others had already
+  found saved me from calling their findings mine.
+
+**Next:** the same study on EVM chains.
+
 If something in this is wrong, please tell me, by an issue on the repository. The
 register has a section for corrections, and it has nine entries.

+
+Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on its Devnet test network. But what it hides is narrower than the word suggests: amounts, not relationships.
+
+XLS-96, the XRP Ledger's standard for confidential transfers, is final. As I write this it is switched on only on Devnet, not on Mainnet or Testnet. I built the core of a receivables facility on it, a bank paying suppliers early against their invoices, and ran it to see exactly what an outside observer can read.
+
+Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each transfer between confidential balances. In the facility, that is each supplier's limit, how much it draws and what it owes.
+
+Public: who pays whom, when and how often. Every amount moved into or out of confidential form, including the size of the float and of each part of it converted back at the end. And some zero balances, which anyone can recognise.
+
+The token's issuer can read every balance, always. No setting turns that off. For a holder, that is where the privacy ends.
+
+Keys cannot be rotated or recovered, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.
+
+I started the same study on EVM chains at the same time. Those results will follow.
+
+Where it could, the project ran its claims on the ledger instead of reading the specification, and it says which ones it only read. It keeps a public register of what it may claim and what it got wrong, and it filed eleven issues with the XRPLF repositories on GitHub. Five are resolved upstream so far.
+
+It is a research project on a test network: not audited, not production-ready.
+
+The write-up: https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
 A read-only demo: https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app
 The code and the claims register: https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions
 
 XLS-96 is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, and its send proof builds on Tess Dore and Murat Cenk's compact sigma protocol.
+
+Independent work; not affiliated with Ripple.

+# X (single long post)
+
+Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on Devnet, under XLS-96. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it to see exactly what it hides. The short answer: amounts, not relationships.
+
+Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each Send between confidential balances.
+
+Public: who pays whom, when and how often. Every amount converted into or out of confidential form. And some zero balances: the ledger writes a fixed encryption of zero, which anyone can recompute from public inputs, for a new balance, an inbox just merged and a position clawed back. I matched it byte for byte against live Devnet state.
+
+The issuer reads every balance, always. XLS-96 keeps a second copy encrypted to the issuer's key, and no setting turns it off. If the token allows clawback, the issuer can also destroy a confidential balance.
+
+Keys are for life: no rotation or recovery in XLS-96, or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.
+
+In the facility, that means the float, which suppliers drew on which days, and every tranche retired at the end are public. Each supplier's limit, draws and what it owes are not, though the public totals still bound them.
+
+Eleven issues went upstream to the XRPLF repositories; five are resolved so far. The write-up's claims cite rows of a public claims register, and the register keeps its own corrections.
+
+I started the same study on EVM chains at the same time. Those results will follow.
+
+A research project on Devnet: not audited, not production-ready.
+
+Write-up: https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
+Demo: https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app
+Code: https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions
+
+Independent work; not affiliated with Ripple.

+# Bluesky (single post)
+
+Confidential transfers on the XRP Ledger (XLS-96), run on Devnet: they hide balances and transfer amounts. Not who pays whom, when, the amounts going in and out, or anything from the issuer. Same study on EVM next.
+
+https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
+
+# Mastodon (single post)
+
+I ran XLS-96, the XRP Ledger's confidential transfers, on Devnet to see what it actually hides. Balances, and the amounts sent between confidential balances. Not who pays whom, when or how often, not the amounts going in and out, and not some zero balances. The token's issuer can read every balance, and no setting turns that off. Open source, with a public register of every claim and correction. The same study on EVM chains comes next.
+
+https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
+
+#XRPL #privacy #cryptography
+
+# Nostr (single note)
+
+Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on its Devnet, under a standard called XLS-96. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it to find out exactly what it hides. The short answer: amounts, not relationships.
+
+Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each transfer between confidential balances.
+
+Public: who pays whom, when and how often; every amount moved into or out of confidential form; and some zero balances, which anyone can recompute from public inputs. I matched that fixed encryption of zero byte for byte against live Devnet state.
+
+It is confidentiality from the public, not from the issuer. The token's issuer reads every balance, always, and no setting turns that off. If the token allows clawback, the issuer can destroy a confidential balance, and unless the token's flags were fixed when it was created, it can turn on locking later and freeze one.
+
+Keys are for life: no rotation or recovery in XLS-96, or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.
+
+I started the same study on EVM chains at the same time. Those results will follow.
+
+A research project on Devnet, not audited and not production-ready. Eleven issues went upstream; five are resolved so far.
+
+Write-up: https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
+Code: https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions
+
+#XRPL #privacy #zeroknowledge
+
+# Self-reply with figure 2 (X and Mastodon, optional)
+
+Who can read what, in one table. Anyone sees who pays whom and every amount going in or out. Only the holder's keys can spend a balance. The issuer reads every balance and every transfer amount.

+<?xml version="1.0"?>
+<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 900 470" role="img" aria-labelledby="title desc" font-family="'Source Sans Pro', -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
+  <title id="title">The receivables facility, as it ran on Devnet</title>
+  <desc id="desc">The facility's flow. Top row: the bank, which issues the token and reads every balance, funds the Dedicated Account, an ordinary account holding the float, with a public payment; the Dedicated Account makes one Convert of the whole float, amount public, so the float is now confidential. Middle, highlighted: drawdowns and repayments are Sends between the confidential float and suppliers A, B and C; the amounts are hidden, and who and when are public; each supplier's limit, draws and what it owes are hidden. Left: each supplier enrols with a small public payment and its own Convert, both amounts public. Bottom: at the end, what is left of the float is retired in tranches, and each ConvertBack's amount is public, giving a public balance again. Footer: the public totals still bound the hidden amounts, and in a small enough book they can pin them exactly.</desc>

22:| P-1 | That this work makes XRPL quantum-safe or quantum-resistant | It does not |
23:| P-2 | That an application-layer PQ scheme protects funds at the ledger level | An adversary who breaks secp256k1 signs a valid classical transaction and the network accepts it |
24:| P-3 | That any amendment is live or enabled, without a dated `feature` RPC check | Amendment state is a reading, not knowledge |
25:| P-4 | That a Confidential MPT demo hides identities | It hides amounts and balances. Sender and receiver remain public |
26:| P-5 | That anything here is trustless, non-custodial, decentralised, audited, production-ready or secure | None of it is; ADR-0001 names the trusted parties |
27:| P-6 | That anything is compliant with regulation in a named jurisdiction | Not a compliance project |
28:| P-7 | That analysis of published work is original research | Cite Cenk, Malhotra, Akinyele, Chen, Xie, Qian by name where the work is theirs. **Add Tess Dore (2026-08-16):** the compact sigma protocol, the twisted-ElGamal analysis and the Bulletproofs++ analysis are Dore & Cenk, RippleX Research — Dore is *not* an XLS-0096 author and is easy to omit by copying E-1's list |
29:| P-8 | Any benchmark number without hardware, parameter set and methodology | Includes re-quoting XLS-0096 §14.2's "laptop-class CPU" timings — see B-1 |

114:| E-63 | **A passive full-ledger observer holding no keys recovered the difference between two confidential amounts, when the ElGamal encryption randomness `r` was reused across two Sends.** `C₁ = r·G` repeats on chain and is visible; subtracting the two `C₂` values annihilates the shared `r·pk_ᵢ` term, leaving `(m − m′)·G`, and a bounded discrete-log search returns the difference. ⚠ **This recovers the DIFFERENCE, not either amount, and it requires a signer bug — reusing `r`. 478:| F-17 | **`cmpt-compact-sigma.pdf` Remark 6.1's stated justification is false, and a reader who trusts it builds a key-extraction bug.** The paper justifies its nonce construction with *"Including the full witness ensures nonces are unique per transaction."* **The witness is byte-identical across a resequenced or version-bumped resubmission of the same transfer**, while `TransactionContextID` — and therefore the challenge — is not. 479:| F-18 | **The published Rust FFI crate silently links an mpt-crypto four tag-generations behind rippled's, and it is not on the mainline branch.** `mpt-crypto-sys@0.1.0-beta.1` sets `MPT_CRYPTO_VERSION = "0.3.0-rc2"` and downloads a prebuilt-dylib release tarball under a SHA-256 pin. `0.3.0-rc2` (commit `83d9b13`) is **older than the `0.4.0-rc4` shipped in rippled 3.3.0**, and older than `1.0.2` and `1.0.4`. **Two distinct failure modes, and they are opposite in character.** (i) Left alone, `cargo build` **succeeds** and links `0.3.0-rc2` — the crate's vendored `secp256k1_mpt.h` is **byte-identical** to the header in the tarball it fetches, so nothing is inconsistent and nothing warns; you simply get an old prover. (ii) Redirected at a current library via `MPT_CRYPTO_LIB_DIR` (→ E-61), the drift becomes loud: the `0.3.0-rc2` header declares **seven functions that no longer exist at `1.0.4`** — `secp256k1_elgamal_pedersen_link_prove`/`_verify`, `secp256k1_equality_plaintext_prove`/`_verify`, `secp256k1_mpt_proof_equality_shared_r_size`, `secp256k1_mpt_prove_equality_shared_r`, `secp256k1_mpt_verify_equality_shared_r` — so a caller touching any of them gets undefined symbols. **Upstream removed exported functions between the pinned version and current**, which is the direction that matters: the stale side has *more* API, not less. Separately, both crates were published from `XRPLF/xrpl-rust` commit `d36ef38`, path `internal/mpt-crypto-sys`, and **`d36ef38` is the head of the unmerged branch `mpt-crypto-beta-release` only** — the path does not exist on `main` or at the `v1.2.0` release | Verified 2026-08-18 by downloading the crate and the `0.3.0-rc2` natives tarball (20 MB, prebuilt dylibs for six platforms; the fetch path **works**, contrary to a first reading here that it might 404), diffing headers, and resolving the publish commit's branch membership via the GitHub API. Crates.io re-queried the same day: still exactly one version each, 2026-06-08 (E-57). ⚠ **Failure mode (ii) is read, not executed** — no Rust binary was linked, so which of the seven a real signer would touch is undetermined. 513:| R-3 | F-3: "docs say confidentiality can be toggled on and off" | Withdrawn 2026-08-16 | Corrected upstream. The canonical xrpl.org page states enabling is one-way |
514:| R-4 | F-4: "docs say clawback resets the version counter" | Withdrawn 2026-08-16 | Not a doc error. TOB-RIPCTX-11, a Medium implementation bug found by Trail of Bits in April 2026 and since Resolved. The prerelease docs described pre-fix behaviour |
515:| R-6 | B-11 / ADR-0002 blocker 3 / investigation §12: that encrypted loan accounting is **structurally** blocked, because XLS-96's additive homomorphism "cannot support amortisation, which multiplies a balance by a rate" | Withdrawn 2026-08-17. The residual true statement is B-11 as rewritten | **The mathematics was wrong.** Scalar multiplication by a *public* scalar is native to an additively homomorphic scheme: for `(C₁,C₂) = (rG, mG+rP)`, scaling both components by public `k` yields `(krG, kmG+krP)`, which decrypts to `k·m`. An interest rate is a public loan parameter. What is genuinely non-linear is rounding and fixed-point truncation — and the remedy for that is a per-payment ZK proof, which is the pattern XLS-96 already uses. **Found independently by both REVIEW-003 legs**, and verified algebraically before acceptance. It was graded C and its inference was stated, which is what made it checkable — but a stated inference that is wrong is still wrong |
516:| R-5 | TASK ZERO §9: the vault converts the whole facility float in one transaction | ~~Retracted 2026-08-16 per ADDENDUM §1~~ — **un-retracted 2026-08-16 (same day), see F-7** | The retraction was correct about the mechanism and wrong about the consequence. A 10,000,000-unit balance is **not** undecryptable: decryption takes a caller-supplied window, and the vault — which tracks its own float off-ledger anyway — decrypts it in ~5 ms with a narrow window. §9's single-conversion design **stands**. What must be added is not a float ceiling but a **balance-tracking requirement** and a resynchronisation cost budget |
517:| R-7 | `docs/explainer/WHAT-CONFIDENTIAL-MEANS-2026-09-02.md`, limit 1, and the README before 2026-10-19: a holder who converts in 500, receives nothing and converts back 400 shows that *"100 left by transfer"* | The other 100 is either still held or has left by confidential transfer. The arithmetic bounds the balance and does not say which. Corrected in the explainer on 2026-10-21 | The README's rewrite for publication (`c561541`, 2026-10-19) carried the corrected sentence with no row, and the explainer the README links for the long form kept the old one, public from that day. Found on 2026-10-21 while drafting the hosted site's explainer from both. The error overstated what an observer learns, not what is hidden |
518:| R-8 | `web/api/capability.ts`'s wallet row and the wallet page: *"A confidential transaction needs the ElGamal secret and the account key"*, and *"needs two secrets"* | A Send, a ConvertBack and the first Convert, which registers the key, need both; a MergeInbox or a later Convert needs only the account key (TASK ZERO §3), and the facility signs its MergeInbox with the seed alone. The wallet conclusion stands, because without the first Convert there is no position. Corrected 2026-10-22 | Found by `REVIEW-061` leg A in a diagram caption that repeated the sentence. Both copies had been on the public site since publication; earlier reads of the wallet page checked its conclusion, which holds, and not this premise |
519:| R-9 | The hosted explainer `/how-it-works`, `README.md` and `WHAT-CONFIDENTIAL-MEANS`, the last as *"the sentence to use"*: ~~*"it hides the shape of the book, not its size"*~~ | *"It hides how much each supplier draws and owes, not who borrows, when, or the size of the float."* Replaced 2026-10-22, and `check-disclosure-phrases` now refuses the old wording unless it is struck beside this id | True as the register meant it, the per-supplier amounts against the public totals. `REVIEW-062`'s leg B, reading the draft blog post as a stranger, took *shape* to mean who borrows, when and how often, which is public, so the sentence overstated the privacy in the direction P-4 and P-11 forbid. It was in the README and `WHAT-CONFIDENTIAL-MEANS` from 2026-09-02 (`00b5478`) and on the hosted explainer from E-350, and every earlier read passed it, because each read it as its row |

Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on its Devnet test network. But what it hides is narrower than the word suggests: amounts, not relationships.

XLS-96, the XRP Ledger's standard for confidential transfers, is final. As I write this it is switched on only on Devnet, not on Mainnet or Testnet. I built the core of a receivables facility on it, a bank paying suppliers early against their invoices, and ran it to see exactly what an outside observer can read.

Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each transfer between confidential balances. In the facility, that is each supplier's limit, how much it draws and what it owes.

Public: who pays whom, when and how often. Every amount moved into or out of confidential form, including the size of the float and of each part of it converted back at the end. And some zero balances, which anyone can recognise.

The token's issuer can read every balance, always. No setting turns that off. For a holder, that is where the privacy ends.

Keys cannot be rotated or recovered, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.

I started the same study on EVM chains at the same time. Those results will follow.

Where it could, the project ran its claims on the ledger instead of reading the specification, and it says which ones it only read. It keeps a public register of what it may claim and what it got wrong, and it filed eleven issues with the XRPLF repositories on GitHub. Five are resolved upstream so far.

It is a research project on a test network: not audited, not production-ready.

The write-up: https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
A read-only demo: https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app
The code and the claims register: https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions

XLS-96 is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, and its send proof builds on Tess Dore and Murat Cenk's compact sigma protocol.

Independent work; not affiliated with Ripple.

# X (single long post)

Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on Devnet, under XLS-96. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it to see exactly what it hides. The short answer: amounts, not relationships.

Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each Send between confidential balances.

Public: who pays whom, when and how often. Every amount converted into or out of confidential form. And some zero balances: the ledger writes a fixed encryption of zero, which anyone can recompute from public inputs, for a new balance, an inbox just merged and a position clawed back. I matched it byte for byte against live Devnet state.

The issuer reads every balance, always. XLS-96 keeps a second copy encrypted to the issuer's key, and no setting turns it off. If the token allows clawback, the issuer can also destroy a confidential balance.

Keys are for life: no rotation or recovery in XLS-96, or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.

In the facility, that means the float, which suppliers drew on which days, and every tranche retired at the end are public. Each supplier's limit, draws and what it owes are not, though the public totals still bound them.

Eleven issues went upstream to the XRPLF repositories; five are resolved so far. The write-up's claims cite rows of a public claims register, and the register keeps its own corrections.

I started the same study on EVM chains at the same time. Those results will follow.

A research project on Devnet: not audited, not production-ready.

Write-up: https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
Demo: https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app
Code: https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions

Independent work; not affiliated with Ripple.

# Nostr (single note)

Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on its Devnet, under a standard called XLS-96. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it to find out exactly what it hides. The short answer: amounts, not relationships.

Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each transfer between confidential balances.

     4	excerpt: "XLS-96 lets a token holder keep balances encrypted on the public XRP Ledger. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it on Devnet to see exactly where the line falls. It hides how much moves inside confidential form. It does not hide who pays whom, when, the amounts at the edges, or anything from the issuer."

    15	
    16	*Status, before anything else: a research project on the XRP Ledger's Devnet test
    17	network. Not audited, not production-ready, and not safe to put value behind. Its
    18	signer refuses every network but Devnet.*
    19	
    20	> **Provenance.** Ids such as *E-58* below are rows in the project's claims register,
    21	> [`CLAIMS.md`](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions/blob/main/CLAIMS.md).
    22	> Each row says what supports it: a transaction run on Devnet, a line of source, or a
    23	> document read on a stated date. If this post and a row ever disagree, trust the row.
    24	
    25	---
    26	
    27	Can a token move confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, under a standard called
    28	XLS-96, and today only on Devnet. A new feature reaches the XRP Ledger as an
    29	amendment, which a network's validators switch on. When I checked on 22 October
    30	2026, XLS-96's amendment, `ConfidentialTransfer`, was enabled on Devnet, and
    31	supported but not enabled on Mainnet and Testnet. That reading goes stale; the
    32	repository has a script that takes a fresh one.
    33	
    34	What XLS-96 hides is narrower than the word *confidential* suggests. It hides
    35	balances, and the amounts of transfers between confidential balances. It does not
    36	hide who pays whom, when, or how often. It does not hide amounts entering or
    37	leaving confidential form. And it hides nothing from the token's issuer.
    38	
    39	I set out to find exactly where that line falls by running transactions rather
    40	than by reading the specification, and I started the same study on two ledgers at
    41	once: the XRP Ledger, and EVM chains. This post is the XRP Ledger half. The EVM
    42	results will follow in a separate post.
    43	
    44	The XRP Ledger project is called W-CONF. Its code and claims register are public at
    45	[github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions),
    46	and a read-only demo is at
    47	[xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app](https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app).
    48	
    49	---
    50	
    51	## What XLS-96 is, briefly
    52	
    53	The XRP Ledger is public: anyone can read every account and every transaction.
    54	Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its token types: an account issues a
    55	token, and other accounts hold it. XLS-96, Confidential Transfers for MPTs, lets a
    56	holder keep an MPT balance encrypted on that public ledger.
    57	
    58	Each confidential balance is an ElGamal ciphertext, a public-key encryption of the
    59	amount. A holder registers their own encryption key when they opt in. The ledger
    60	still has to stop anyone spending more than they hold, so every transaction that
    61	spends from a confidential balance carries zero-knowledge proofs, which validators
    62	check without learning the amount.
    63	
    64	A position moves through four transactions:
    65	
    66	- **Convert** moves tokens from a public balance into the holder's confidential
    67	  inbox. The amount is published.
    68	- **Send** moves an amount from one confidential balance into another holder's
    69	  inbox. The amount is hidden. The sender and receiver are not.
    70	- **MergeInbox** moves the inbox into the balance the holder can spend. Arrivals
    71	  wait in the inbox so that they cannot change a balance while a proof about it is
    72	  being built, and they cannot be sent until they are merged.
    73	- **ConvertBack** moves tokens back to a public balance. The amount is published.
    74	
    75	Only Send hides an amount.
    76	
    77	The specification, XLS-0096, is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo
    78	Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, and is a final standard (E-1). The
    79	compact sigma protocol, one of the zero-knowledge proofs behind a Send, is the work
    80	of Tess Dore and Murat Cenk at RippleX Research. The reference cryptography is
    81	[`XRPLF/mpt-crypto`](https://github.com/XRPLF/mpt-crypto). This project builds on
    82	their work and claims none of it.
    83	
    84	Upstream's code has had three outside reviews. None of them reviewed this project,
    85	which has had no outside audit. Trail of Bits reviewed upstream's Confidential
    86	Transfer implementation in April 2026; that report is the one I could read and
    87	check my findings against, and a later revision of it could not be obtained. The
    88	Sherlock XRP Ledger Attackathon was a contest that covered Confidential Transfers,
    89	and its findings are not public. A Zellic scan of mpt-crypto is known to me only
    90	through three identifiers an upstream issue cites. Of the three reviews, only Trail
    91	of Bits' April report could be checked.
    92	
    93	---
    94	
    95	## What it hides, and what it does not
    96	
    97	<figure>
    98	  <img src="/images/posts/amounts-not-relationships/figure-1-where-the-line-falls.svg" alt="A token balance moves left to right. A public balance; an arrow labelled Convert, amount public, into a panel of confidential balances where holder A sends to holder B: the amount is hidden, the sender and receiver are public, and each balance is hidden unless it is visibly zero; an arrow labelled ConvertBack, amount public, out to a public balance. Below: public everywhere, who sends to whom, when and how often, and the total held in confidential form. The issuer reads every confidential balance, as does an auditor if the token names one, and no setting turns this off. A balance is visibly zero when it is new, when its inbox was just merged, or after a clawback.">
    99	  <figcaption>Figure 1. Amounts are hidden inside confidential form and public at its edges. Who pays whom is public everywhere, and the issuer reads every balance.</figcaption>
   100	</figure>
   101	
   102	**Hidden from the public:** each holder's balance, and the amount of each Send.
   103	
   104	**Public, always:**
   105	
   106	- The sender and receiver of every transfer, and when it happened, so how often
   107	  anyone transacts (P-4, P-11).
   108	- Every amount converted in or out, each one separately.
   109	- The token's total supply, and the total held in confidential form.
   110	- That a balance is exactly zero, in three cases, below.
   111	
   112	**Who can read every balance:** the issuer, always. XLS-96 keeps a second copy of
   113	each confidential balance, encrypted to the issuer's key, and no setting turns it
   114	off (P-9). An auditor can read them too, if the token names one, and only one is
   115	supported (E-11). I ran this rather than inferring it. The holder, the issuer and
   116	the auditor each decrypted the same balance, 500, and each read 475 after a
   117	25-unit Send (E-58).
   118	
   119	**Who can spend:** only whoever holds the holder's encryption secret, because a
   120	Send's proof cannot be made without it (E-33). Where that secret is derived from
   121	the account's master seed, as this project derives it, whoever holds the seed holds
   122	the secret too. The issuer cannot spend a holder's balance. If the token allows
   123	clawback, a setting that lets an issuer take tokens back, the issuer can destroy a
   124	confidential balance, crediting no one, and this project's tokens allow clawback
   125	(E-12). Unless the token's flags were made unchangeable when it was created, the
   126	issuer can also turn on locking later and freeze balances. That second power I read
   127	in rippled's source and did not run (E-290).
   128	
   129	<figure>
   130	  <img src="/images/posts/amounts-not-relationships/figure-2-who-can-read-who-can-spend.svg" alt="A table of who can see what. Columns: who pays whom and when; amounts converted in or out; a holder's balance; a Send's amount; can spend a balance. Anyone: yes, yes, only whether it is visibly zero, no, no. A holder: yes, yes, their own, their own, their own with both their keys. The issuer, highlighted: yes, yes, every one, every one, and no, though it can destroy one by clawback and may freeze one. An auditor, if the token names one: yes, yes, every one, every one, no.">
   131	  <figcaption>Figure 2. Who can read what, and who can spend. A dashed cell is a partial yes.</figcaption>
   132	</figure>
   133	
   134	**Zero is sometimes visible.** XLS-96 writes a fixed encryption of zero, which
   135	anyone can recompute from public inputs, in three places: a new confidential
   136	balance, an inbox that a MergeInbox has just emptied, and a position clawed back.
   137	So enrolment is publicly visible. The English documentation said this value could
   138	not be told apart from other ciphertexts. I recomputed it from public inputs and
   139	matched it byte for byte against live Devnet state (F-1, E-59), reported it, and the
   140	English page was corrected. A balance spent down to zero holds a randomised
   141	encryption of zero, and is not recognisable (E-211).
   142	
   143	**The public numbers bound the hidden ones.** If a holder converts in 500, receives
   144	nothing, and converts back 400, anyone can work out that the other 100 is either
   145	still held or has left by confidential Send. No key is needed. I first wrote that
   146	the 100 *"left by transfer"*. That overstated what an observer learns, and it is
   147	recorded as a correction (R-7).
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## No rotation, no recovery
   152	
   153	A registered key can never be changed (E-9). XLS-96 has no key rotation and no key
   154	recovery (P-10). If a holder loses their key, and any seed it could be re-derived
   155	from, the balance cannot be spent. The only remedy is an issuer clawback, which
   156	destroys the balance.
   157	
   158	A draft standard, XLS-99, by Aanchal Malhotra and Yinyi Qian, proposes rotation for
   159	holder, issuer and auditor keys, and recovery from key loss. When I checked, rippled
   160	declared its amendment as not supported, in its development branch and in its
   161	latest release candidate, and Mainnet, Testnet and Devnet did not know it (E-353).
   162	So there is no rotation or recovery in XLS-96, or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet,
   163	today.
   164	
   165	---
   166	
   167	## The example: a confidential receivables facility
   168	
   169	To test the standard against something with stakes, I built the core of a
   170	receivables facility. A bank pays a large buyer's suppliers early, against their
   171	invoices. How much a supplier draws says a lot about its cash position, so these
   172	amounts are commercially sensitive.
   173	
   174	The bank issues a token. An ordinary XRPL account, which this project calls the
   175	Dedicated Account, holds the float, the money the facility advances, and converts it
   176	into confidential form once. Suppliers enrol, draw down by confidential Send, and
   177	repay the same way. At the end, what is left of the float is retired in several
   178	parts, called tranches, by ConvertBack. It ran on Devnet in 28 validated facility
   179	transactions, besides setting up the token (E-146).
   180	
   181	<figure>
   182	  <img src="/images/posts/amounts-not-relationships/figure-3-the-facility.svg" alt="The facility's flow. The bank, which issues the token and reads every balance, funds the Dedicated Account with a public payment. The Dedicated Account makes one Convert of the whole float, amount public, so the float is confidential. Drawdowns and repayments are Sends between the float and suppliers A, B and C: amounts hidden, who and when public; each supplier's limit, draws and what it owes are hidden. Each supplier enrols with a small public payment and its own Convert, both amounts public. At the end, what is left of the float is retired in tranches, and each ConvertBack's amount is public. The public totals still bound the hidden amounts.">
   183	  <figcaption>Figure 3. The facility as it ran on Devnet. The amounts that move between the float and the suppliers are hidden; the amounts at the edges are not.</figcaption>
   184	</figure>
   185	
   186	**Anyone can see** the size of the float, because converting it publishes the
   187	amount. They can see which suppliers enrolled, who drew and repaid, on which days,
   188	and how often. And they can see the size of every retirement tranche, because each
   189	ConvertBack publishes its own amount (F-24). My own walkthrough first said a
   190	ConvertBack published only *"the aggregate change"*. The validated transactions
   191	showed each tranche in plaintext.
   192	
   193	**Hidden from the public:** each supplier's limit, the size of each drawdown and
   194	repayment, and what each supplier still owes. The bank, as issuer, sees all of it.
   195	The public totals still bound these amounts, and in a small enough book they can pin
   196	them exactly.
   197	
   198	So it hides how much each supplier draws and owes. It does not hide who borrows,
   199	when, how often, or the size of the whole. An early version of the design claimed
   200	the facility *"shows nothing about which supplier drew how much"* (R-1). Which
   201	supplier drew, and when, is public.
   202	
   203	Two limits of that run. First, it read the ledger through a public Devnet node. The
   204	design requires a node on the same machine, and a local Devnet node never finished
   205	syncing on the hardware I had, so I accepted that as a named risk (E-148, E-151).
   206	The run says nothing about that requirement. Second, one test driver played the
   207	bank and every supplier and held every seed. The run shows that these transactions
   208	are well formed and that rippled accepts them. It does not show how custody would
   209	work.
   210	
   211	---
   212	
   213	## Reading the specification, and running it
   214	
   215	Several of the things above I learned only by running them:
   216	
   217	- That three different keys decrypt the same balance, through a change (E-58).
   218	- That the encryption of zero matches a value anyone can recompute (F-1).
   219	- That a balance spent to zero is not recognisable. My own observer page had
   220	  labelled every ciphertext that was not the fixed zero as *"Non-zero"*, and a
   221	  holder whose balance decrypted to 0 disproved it (E-211).
   222	- That a failing transaction is not simply rejected. A `tec` result, one class of
   223	  XRPL failure code, is still applied to the ledger: the fee is charged and the
   224	  account's sequence number is used, though what the transaction asked for does not
   225	  happen. The submission parameter `fail_hard` asks the node to discard it instead.
   226	  I ran both on Devnet with a plain Payment that fails with `tecNO_AUTH`: the same
   227	  signed bytes were applied without the flag, and discarded with it (E-149).
   228	
   229	That last one matters more for confidential transactions than for plain ones,
   230	because a `tec` keeps the transaction's fields, ciphertexts included. If a signer
   231	reads a wrong destination key from a dishonest node, the amount is published
   232	encrypted to that key for good, even though the transaction fails. That case I read
   233	in rippled's source and did not run (F-23).
   234	
   235	Running is not a substitute for reading what others have already found. Several
   236	things I first recorded as findings turned out to be issues that Trail of Bits'
   237	review had already found and Ripple had fixed.
   238	
   239	---
   240	
   241	## What the reviews caught
   242	
   243	Design decisions and fixes went through rounds of adversarial review. These were
   244	the project's own reviews: not outside audits, and not reviews by outside security
   245	professionals. Each round gave its review passes deliberately different material,
   246	so that their agreement would mean more than one reading copied three times. The
   247	repository keeps more than sixty numbered review records, including the ones that
   248	found me wrong. A few of the catches:
   249	
   250	- **A secret not wiped from memory, behind a comment explaining why it could not
   251	  be.** The comment said the secret's type belonged to an outside library. It was
   252	  the project's own type, and one search of its file showed it had no wiping at all
   253	  (E-200).
   254	- **A design claim that four review passes independently ruled unsound.** I had
   255	  written that the project's local read-only web viewer *"moves no trust
   256	  boundary"*. It added no signing authority. But it re-served, to any local user,
   257	  data the project protects with file permissions (E-230). That was the viewer that
   258	  runs on the holder's machine, before the hosted demo existed; the demo serves only
   259	  static files.
   260	- **A release gate that passed a Content Security Policy every browser refused.**
   261	  The gate hashed inline scripts over the file's bytes. Browsers hash the text they
   262	  parse, which differs. Only loading the pages in a real browser showed it (E-334).
   263	- **Fixes that did not fix.** In one review's second round, five of the first
   264	  round's fixes had not discharged their findings. Only the review pass that ran
   265	  each finding's own example against the fixed code found them (E-345).
   266	
   267	The lesson I keep relearning: fixing something and describing the fix are two acts
   268	that fail separately. A review that reads my summary of a finding will tick the
   269	summary.
   270	
   271	---
   272	
   273	## Checks that catch a false sentence
   274	
   275	The working rule is that a claim needs its evidence before it is written. The
   276	claims register holds each established claim with what supports it, and twelve
   277	standing prohibitions, P-1 to P-12, on what may not be claimed at all: that XLS-96
   278	hides identities, that holders are private from the issuer, that it supports key
   279	rotation, any benchmark without its hardware and method, and any claim that a
   280	source does *not* say something without the search that would show otherwise.
   281	
   282	Prose drifts anyway, so some of it is enforced by checks that run in CI. One fails
   283	when a retracted phrase reappears without its correction. One fails when a note
   284	meant for upstream says something is missing from a source and does not record the
   285	search that found it missing. One keeps the register's derived indexes in step with
   286	it.
   287	
   288	They do not catch everything. The register keeps nine correction records, R-1 to
   289	R-9. Most withdraw or narrow something this project claimed; one records a
   290	retraction that was itself reversed. R-8 said every confidential transaction needs
   291	both of a holder's keys, when a MergeInbox needs only the account key; it was on the
   292	public demo until a review pass found it repeated in a diagram caption. R-9 came
   293	from reviewing this post. The README and the demo summarised the facility as hiding
   294	*"the shape of the book, not its size"*, and a reader new to the project took
   295	*shape* to mean who borrows and when, which is public. That sentence is replaced
   296	everywhere, and a check now refuses it.
   297	
   298	At one point the register still listed as open four filings that upstream had
   299	already fixed (E-316). Nothing re-checked them until I surveyed every filing at
   300	source. That survey now runs before anything I publish about them, this post
   301	included.
   302	
   303	---
   304	
   305	## What went upstream
   306	
   307	This project has filed eleven issues in four XRPLF repositories. Their state when I
   308	checked, read at source (E-353):
   309	
   310	- **Four resolved.** Three issues against the XLS-0096 text were resolved in the
   311	  merged standard. The documentation's sentence calling the zero value
   312	  indistinguishable was corrected on the English page. The Japanese translation was
   313	  made from the text before the fix, and still carries it.
   314	- **The mpt-crypto build.** Its lockfile pinned an OpenSSL revision that the
   315	  documented package remote did not serve. Fixed on mpt-crypto's main branch, not
   316	  yet in a release. I re-ran the check against the merged commit, and it resolves.
   317	- **The fixed zero, from JavaScript.** mpt-crypto's WASM and npm packages did not
   318	  expose the function that computes the fixed encryption of zero, which is the check
   319	  an outside observer most needs. A maintainer agreed and a pull request is approved
   320	  and not merged. I have offered to write the JavaScript wrapper once it is
   321	  released.
   322	- **Three filed most recently, against mpt-crypto, with no reply yet:** an
   323	  ambiguity in what the compact sigma paper's nonce input covers; a WASM build
   324	  script that fails outside its pinned toolchain; and a proof-size total in the
   325	  paper that assumes a ciphertext component is sent once, where rippled and XLS-0096
   326	  send it per recipient.
   327	- **A question to XRPL-Standards**, whether a confidential balance is meant to stay
   328	  invisible to the accounting of the ledger's vaults (XLS-65), which pool one asset
   329	  and issue shares against it, has had no reply in nearly two months.
   330	- **A filing to rippled that listed only things done well** was closed without
   331	  comment the day it was filed, so its reason is not known. It also fit neither of
   332	  that repository's two issue templates, and the project's filing rules now forbid a
   333	  positives-only filing to a bug tracker.
   334	
   335	I do not call any of these new, or unreported. Of the three outside reviews of
   336	upstream's code, I could check my findings against one.
   337	
   338	---
   339	
   340	## What it does not show
   341	
   342	- **No run against a local node.** Every Devnet read went to the public cluster
   343	  (E-151).
   344	- **Custody is accepted, not solved.** The issuer can erase or freeze the facility's
   345	  float. The Dedicated Account's key both moves the float and decrypts every amount
   346	  sent to or from it, so those two powers cannot be held apart (E-266).
   347	- **The key derivation is unpublished.** It is specified in this repository only, so
   348	  a holder with their master seed but not this repository cannot reconstruct their
   349	  key. Treat it as lock-in until it is published.
   350	- **A hostile process running as the same user** can read the encryption secret out
   351	  of memory.
   352	
   353	---
   354	
   355	## Try it
   356	
   357	The demo is static pages built from one snapshot of Devnet. It signs nothing and
   358	holds no keys. It shows what an observer reads of four test accounts, including
   359	which balances are visibly zero; which encrypted copies the issuer can read, without
   360	publishing the figures; and what each kind of key can do. It does not show the
   361	facility, whose record is in the repository.
   362	
   363	To transact, you run the signer yourself, on your own machine. The README explains
   364	how to build it and run the local version of the site. It does not yet walk through
   365	creating a holder profile and funded Devnet accounts, which a transaction needs.
   366	
   367	The repository has the Rust signer, the TypeScript facility, the read-only web
   368	viewer, the claims register and the review records, under Apache-2.0.
   369	
   370	---
   371	
   372	## What to take from it
   373	
   374	- **XLS-96 hides amounts, not relationships.** Balances and Send amounts are
   375	  hidden from the public. Who pays whom, when and how often is not.
   376	- **The edges are public.** Every Convert and ConvertBack publishes its amount, and
   377	  the totals bound what is hidden.
   378	- **The issuer sees everything.** It reads every balance, can destroy one by
   379	  clawback, and may be able to freeze one.
   380	- **Keys are for life.** No rotation and no recovery, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet,
   381	  Testnet or Devnet today. XLS-99 is a draft that would add both.
   382	- **Running it found things reading did not**, and reading what others had already
   383	  found saved me from calling their findings mine.
   384	
   385	**Next:** the same study on EVM chains.
   386	
   387	If something in this is wrong, please tell me, by an issue on the repository. The
   388	register has a section for corrections, and it has nine entries.
   389

CLAIMS.md:482:| F-26 | ⚠ **The facility walkthrough's *"After this, no plaintext amount appears again until the facility is retired or resized"* was FALSE, and it is the SECOND false disclosure sentence in that document.** Step 5 — supplier enrolment — publishes **two** plaintext amounts per supplier: the bank's `Payment` of the enrolment token, and the supplier's own `ConfidentialMPTConvert`, whose `MPTAmount` is a plaintext field exactly as step 4's and step 9's are. CLAIMS.md:484:| F-28 | ⚠ **`tapFailHard` stops a `tec` reaching the LEDGER. CLAIMS.md:485:| F-23 | **A wrong ledger read is a CONFIDENTIALITY break, not a rejected transaction — and the signer cannot control which.** A `ConfidentialMPTSend` encrypts the amount to the destination's `HolderEncryptionKey` and the issuer's `IssuerEncryptionKey`, both read from the ledger. rippled verifies against the keys **it** holds — `ConfidentialMPTSend.cpp:132` takes `(*sleDestinationMPToken)[sfHolderEncryptionKey]` — so a substituted key fails the proof.      1	/**
     2	 * The hosted demo's diagrams, at the owner's request of 2026-10-22.
     3	 *
     4	 * ⚠ **Markup, not images.** The policy's `style-src 'self'` refuses inline
     5	 * styles, and a diagram drawn in markup reflows on a phone, follows dark mode,
     6	 * and is text the gate reads like any other sentence. So every label is a
     7	 * claim: each restates a sentence already on the page it sits on, or a row the
     8	 * page cites. The words *decrypt* and *plaintext* are not used, for check 8b's
     9	 * reason (see `routes/how-it-works.tsx`).
    10	 *
    11	 * ⚠ **No ledger value.** Only `/observer` and `/issuer` may render one (check
    12	 * 8), and these diagrams render none on any page.
    13	 */
    14	import type { ReactNode } from "react";
    15	
    16	type Tone = "public" | "hidden" | "issuer" | "plain" | "breaks";
    17	
    18	const TONE: Record<Tone, string> = {
    19	  public: "border-amber-400 bg-amber-50 text-amber-950 dark:border-amber-600 dark:bg-amber-950/40 dark:text-amber-100",
    20	  hidden: "border-emerald-500 bg-emerald-50 text-emerald-950 dark:border-emerald-600 dark:bg-emerald-950/40 dark:text-emerald-100",
    21	  issuer: "border-violet-400 bg-violet-50 text-violet-950 dark:border-violet-500 dark:bg-violet-950/40 dark:text-violet-100",
    22	  plain: "border-black/20 dark:border-white/25",
    23	  // The site's warning red, as the custody page's own "breaks" uses.
    24	  breaks: "border-[var(--color-warn)]",
    25	};
    26	
    27	const TONE_WORD: Record<Exclude<Tone, "plain" | "breaks">, string> = {
    28	  public: "public",
    29	  hidden: "hidden from the public",
    30	  issuer: "the issuer can read it",
    31	};
    32	
    33	function Figure({ caption, children }: { caption: string; children: ReactNode }) {
    34	  return (
    35	    <figure className="my-4">
    36	      {children}
    37	      <figcaption className="text-xs opacity-70 mt-2">{caption}</figcaption>
    38	    </figure>
    39	  );
    40	}
    41	
    42	/** A box. `sub` is a short description; `field` is a ledger field name, set in code. */
    43	function Node({ tone = "plain", title, sub, field, children, dashed = false }: {
    44	  tone?: Tone; title: string; sub?: string; field?: string; children?: ReactNode; dashed?: boolean;
    45	}) {
    46	  return (
    47	    <div className={`rounded-md border ${dashed ? "border-dashed" : ""} ${TONE[tone]} p-2 text-xs leading-snug`}>
    48	      <div className="font-semibold">{title}</div>
    49	      {field && <code className="block text-[10px] opacity-70 break-all mt-0.5">{field}</code>}
    50	      {sub && <div className="text-[11px] opacity-80 mt-0.5">{sub}</div>}
    51	      {children && <div className="mt-1">{children}</div>}
    52	    </div>
    53	  );
    54	}
    55	
    56	/** An arrow with its label: across on a wide screen, down on a phone. */
    57	function Edge({ label, tone, always }: { label: string; tone?: Tone; always?: "down" }) {
    58	  const arrow = always === "down"
    59	    ? <span aria-hidden="true">↓</span>
    60	    : <><span aria-hidden="true" className="hidden sm:inline">→</span><span aria-hidden="true" className="sm:hidden">↓</span></>;
    61	  return (
    62	    <div className="flex sm:flex-col items-center justify-center gap-1 text-center text-[11px] leading-tight px-1">
    63	      <span className="text-base opacity-70">{arrow}</span>
    64	      <span className={tone && tone !== "plain" ? `rounded border px-1 ${TONE[tone]}` : "opacity-80"}>{label}</span>
    65	    </div>
    66	  );
    67	}
    68	
    69	function Down({ label, tone }: { label: string; tone?: Tone }) {
    70	  return <Edge label={label} tone={tone} always="down" />;
    71	}
    72	
    73	export function Legend({ tones = ["public", "hidden", "issuer"] }: { tones?: Exclude<Tone, "plain" | "breaks">[] }) {
    74	  return (
    75	    <div className="flex flex-wrap gap-2 text-[11px] mt-1" aria-label="Key to the colours">
    76	      {tones.map((t) => (
    77	        <span key={t} className={`rounded border px-1.5 py-0.5 ${TONE[t]}`}>{TONE_WORD[t]}</span>
    78	      ))}
    79	    </div>
    80	  );
    81	}

    30	
    31	Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on its Devnet test network. But what it hides is narrower than the word suggests: amounts, not relationships.
    32	
    33	XLS-96, the XRP Ledger's standard for confidential transfers, is final. As I write this it is switched on only on Devnet, not on Mainnet or Testnet. I built the core of a receivables facility on it, a bank paying suppliers early against their invoices, and ran it to see exactly what an outside observer can read.
    34	
    35	Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each transfer between confidential balances. In the facility, that is each supplier's limit, how much it draws and what it owes.
    36	
    37	Public: who pays whom, when and how often. Every amount moved into or out of confidential form, including the size of the float and of each part of it converted back at the end. And some zero balances, which anyone can recognise.
    38	
    39	The token's issuer can read every balance, always. No setting turns that off. For a holder, that is where the privacy ends.
    40	
    41	Keys cannot be rotated or recovered, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.
    42	
    43	I started the same study on EVM chains at the same time. Those results will follow.
    44	
    45	Where it could, the project ran its claims on the ledger instead of reading the specification, and it says which ones it only read. It keeps a public register of what it may claim and what it got wrong, and it filed eleven issues with the XRPLF repositories on GitHub. Five are resolved upstream so far.
    46	
    47	It is a research project on a test network: not audited, not production-ready.
    48	
    49	The write-up: https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
    50	A read-only demo: https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app
    51	The code and the claims register: https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions
    52	
    53	XLS-96 is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, and its send proof builds on Tess Dore and Murat Cenk's compact sigma protocol.

    43	Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on Devnet, under XLS-96. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it to see exactly what it hides. The short answer: amounts, not relationships.
    44	
    45	Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each Send between confidential balances.
    46	
    47	Public: who pays whom, when and how often. Every amount converted into or out of confidential form. And some zero balances: the ledger writes a fixed encryption of zero, which anyone can recompute from public inputs, for a new balance, an inbox just merged and a position clawed back. I matched it byte for byte against live Devnet state.
    48	
    49	The issuer reads every balance, always. XLS-96 keeps a second copy encrypted to the issuer's key, and no setting turns it off. If the token allows clawback, the issuer can also destroy a confidential balance.
    50

    52

# A confidential receivables facility on the XRPL — how it actually works

**Date:** 2026-08-20, **revised twice on 2026-08-25 and once on 2026-08-28**
(§5's zero-balance nuance for `CLAIMS.md` **E-211**, §6's build table for the
web tier, and the amendment reading re-dated) — §3 step 4 and §4's table
for `CLAIMS.md` **F-26** (a second false disclosure sentence in this document),
§3 step 9 and §4's table for **F-24**, and §6's build table after architecture
§6 step 7 was **built and executed**. **Devnet only.** Written as the reference
an app, an explainer or a post would be built *from* — not as any of those.

⚠ **The facility now runs, and the row in §6 carries a qualification that must
travel with it**: the run was **not** under `CLAIMS.md` B-15's step-7
conditions, because the ledger source was remote under an amended ruling
(E-151). It is evidence that the transactions are well-formed and that rippled
accepts them. It is **not** evidence about the loopback obligation.

> ## ⚠ Read this box before reusing anything below
>
> **This has not been through the project's publishing protocol.** That protocol
> is deliberately not part of a coding session, and nothing here is cleared for
> external use. Every capability sentence below is written against
> `CLAIMS.md`'s standing prohibitions, and the register is the authority if the
> two ever disagree.
>
> **The one sentence that must survive any rewrite:** this design hides
> **amounts**. It does not hide **who** transacts, **with whom**, **when**, or
> **how often**, and the issuer can decrypt every balance by construction. An
> explainer that leaves that out is not a simplification of this document; it is
> a different and false claim.

---

## 1. The commercial problem, in one paragraph

A large buyer's suppliers want to be paid early; a bank will advance against the
buyer's payables. That is receivables financing, and the numbers in it are
commercially sensitive in a specific way: **a supplier's drawdown level tells you
their cash position.** Put that on a public ledger in plaintext and you have
published every supplier's working-capital stress to their competitors and to
the buyer's other counterparties. Put it on a private ledger and you have given
up most of what a shared ledger was for.

**XLS-0096 Confidential MPTs are an attempt at the middle**: amounts encrypted
on a public chain, with a decryption path reserved for the parties who are
accountable for the book.

## 2. The shape

Three roles, **one issuance**, and every participant holds a confidential
balance in it.

```
      ┌────────────────────────┐
      │  Funding bank          │  issuer of the MPT
      │  · IssuerEncryptionKey │  ── can decrypt EVERY balance, always
      │  · AuditorEncryptionKey│  ── optional second party, same power
      └───────────┬────────────┘
                  │ funds publicly, once
                  ▼
      ┌────────────────────────┐
      │  Dedicated Account     │  an ORDINARY XRPL account
      │  holds the float,      │  (not an XLS-65 Vault — see §7)
      │  confidentially        │
      └───────────┬────────────┘
                  │  ConfidentialMPTSend — amounts hidden
        ┌─────────┼─────────┬─────────┐
        ▼         ▼         ▼         ▼
     supplier  supplier  supplier   ...        each with its own
        A         B         C                  HolderEncryptionKey
```

⚠ **"Dedicated Account", never "vault".** An XLS-65 `Vault` is a different
ledger object, it *cannot* convert to a confidential balance, and the word has
already nearly derailed one reading of the design.

## 3. The walkthrough

A worked example: a bank runs a **£50m** facility for **30 suppliers** of one
large buyer.

### Setup — public, and deliberately so

**Step 1 — the bank creates the issuance.** A Multi-Purpose Token flagged to
hold confidential balances. It sets:

- **`IssuerEncryptionKey`** — mandatory. The bank can decrypt every holder's
  balance. **No configuration removes this**, and any design that assumes
  otherwise is wrong about the protocol.
- **`AuditorEncryptionKey`** — optional. A trustee or supervisor with the same
  visibility.
- **`sfDomainID`** — gates the issuance to a permissioned domain, so only
  credentialled accounts can hold it.

⚠ **`TransferFee` must be zero on a confidential issuance.** Fees and interest
settle off-ledger or as separate confidential transfers. That is a protocol
constraint, not a design choice, and it shapes everything downstream.

**Step 2 — the bank creates a Dedicated Account.** An ordinary XRPL account.
It cannot be the issuer account: **an issuer cannot convert its own issuance
into a confidential balance.** The ledger refuses it outright — this is the
reason the design needs a separate account to hold the float, not a stylistic
preference.

**Step 3 — the bank funds it publicly** with the whole £50m float, as plaintext
MPT.

### The one plaintext moment

**Step 4 — one `ConfidentialMPTConvert`.** This does two things at once: it
registers the Dedicated Account's `HolderEncryptionKey`, and it moves the entire
float into confidentiality.

**The amount is public at this step, and that is the intent.** Facility size is
what the market and the funders are entitled to see.

⚠ **~~After this, no plaintext amount appears again until the facility is
retired or resized.~~ That sentence was FALSE and is struck (2026-08-25,
`CLAIMS.md` F-26).** Step 5 publishes two plaintext amounts **per supplier** —
the bank's `Payment` of the enrolment token, and the supplier's own
`ConfidentialMPTConvert`, whose `MPTAmount` is a plaintext field exactly as step
4's and step 9's are. On a thirty-supplier facility that is sixty plaintext
amounts between the float conversion and the first drawdown.

**What is true, and it is what the design actually buys:** no **drawdown** and
no **repayment** publishes an amount, and those are the numbers that carry the
commercial signal. The plaintext amounts are the enrolment tokens, which are
deliberately nominal and identical, and the facility-level ones — its size, and
each tranche of its retirement.

⚠ This is the **second** false disclosure sentence found in this document

## Findings

### A-1 — HIGH
**Quoted text:** Bluesky: “they hide balances and transfer amounts.”

### 1. LinkedIn

#### 1. First reaction

#### 2. What you understood

#### 3. What reads wrong for this audience
- **"The token's issuer can read every balance, always. No setting turns that off. For a holder, that is where the privacy ends."** In corporate treasury, supply-chain finance, and commercial banking, issuer visibility is not a bug or a failure of privacy—it is a mandatory compliance requirement (AML/BSA, sanction screening, risk management, and regulatory reporting). - **"Keys cannot be rotated or recovered, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet."** Phrased this bluntly without immediate operational context, this sounds like an existential custody and disaster-recovery blocker that would immediately disqualify the technology from enterprise consideration.

> 
> *Does the post answer it?* No. The LinkedIn post mentions only the issuer. The blog post notes that an auditor key is supported (and limited to one), but the LinkedIn post omits this detail.

### Blog Post Review (Click-Through Reader Perspective)

#### 1. Does it deliver what the post promised?
**Yes.** The post delivers on its promises. It provides:
- A clear, rigorously bounded explanation of "amounts, not relationships."
- Exact technical mechanics for why the issuer sees all balances (dual ElGamal encryptions) and why zero balances leak (deterministic, unblinded encryptions of zero on initialization, inbox merge, and clawback).
- Clear verification of Devnet live states matched byte-for-byte.
- A grounded walkthrough of the receivables facility, clearly defining what is hidden (supplier draws, limits, current balances) versus what is public (float size, redemption tranches, transaction timing, counterparty addresses).
- Full provenance via the claims register.

#### 2. Where does it lose you?
The post loses momentum in the final third, specifically around the internal development meta-narrative:
- **"What the reviews caught" & "Checks that catch a false sentence":** These sections abruptly pivot the article from a cryptographic and architectural analysis of XLS-96 into an internal post-mortem of the author's own software engineering practices, CI scripts, and review methodology (e.g., discussions of browser CSP byte hashing, memory-wiping boilerplate, and internal review records R-1 to R-9). While this demonstrates rigorous personal discipline, readers who clicked through to understand *XRPL confidential transfers* will find this jarring and self-indulgent.
- **The rippled positive-filing anecdote:** The mention of filing an issue that listed only positive feedback to rippled, which was summarily closed without comment, reads as extraneous and slightly petty compared to the technical substance of the upstream cryptographic findings.
- **Density of parenthetical claims IDs:** Seeing `(E-58)`, `(P-4)`, `(F-1)`, and `(R-7)` in almost every sentence adds reading friction and interrupts prose flow for anyone outside an academic or formal audit context.

#### 3. What would you cut?
- **Cut or relocate the personal CI/review sections:** Move `"What the reviews caught"` and `"Checks that catch a false sentence"` into a separate blog post or an appendix titled *“Methodology & Internal Verification Log.”*
- **Cut the positive-only issue anecdote:** Remove the paragraph describing the positive-only bug report closed by rippled maintainers.
- **Prune inline IDs:** Move the `(E-xxx)` claim tags to footnotes, margin notes, or hyperlink the relevant phrases directly to `CLAIMS.md` rather than inserting bracketed alphanumeric codes into the narrative text.

#### 4. Is anything missing that the social post led you to expect?
- **A concrete ledger state / transaction excerpt:** The posts promised empirical, hands-on ledger inspection (`"matched it byte for byte against live Devnet state"`). Yet, the blog post abstracts the Devnet data entirely into prose and SVG schematics. A reader expecting to see *what an outside observer actually sees* would benefit immensely from seeing an actual snippet of Devnet ledger JSON or hex (e.g., contrasting the predictable, recomputed encryption of zero against an obfuscated ciphertext).
- **The EVM comparison context:** Every social post ended with `"Same study on EVM next"`, leading the reader to anticipate at least a brief paragraph explaining *why* XLS-96 is being compared to EVM confidential primitives (e.g., contrasting XRPL's native protocol approach with EVM smart-contract-based ZK/FHE approaches). The blog post simply repeats the deferral sentence without providing any architectural context.

- **Bluesky**: technologists, researchers and journalists, many skeptical of crypto,
  interested in privacy and in honest negative results.
- **Mastodon**: free-software and information-security people, privacy-minded, often
  hostile to blockchain marketing, who value plain statements and open source.
- **Nostr**: bitcoiners and privacy advocates, skeptical of Ripple and of issuer-controlled
  tokens, alert to surveillance and to anything that calls a controlled system private.

Then, last, read the blog post as a **reader who clicked through from any of those
posts**: does it deliver what the post promised? Where does it lose you? What would you
cut? Is anything in it missing that the social post led you to expect?

End with the line `END OF LEG B REPORT`.

## LinkedIn post

Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on its Devnet test network. But what it hides is narrower than the word suggests: amounts, not relationships.

XLS-96, the XRP Ledger's standard for confidential transfers, is final. As I write this it is switched on only on Devnet, not on Mainnet or Testnet. I built the core of a receivables facility on it, a bank paying suppliers early against their invoices, and ran it to see exactly what an outside observer can read.

Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each transfer between confidential balances. In the facility, that is each supplier's limit, how much it draws and what it owes.

Public: who pays whom, when and how often. Every amount moved into or out of confidential form, including the size of the float and of each part of it converted back at the end. And some zero balances, which anyone can recognise.

The token's issuer can read every balance, always. No setting turns that off. For a holder, that is where the privacy ends.

Keys cannot be rotated or recovered, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.

I started the same study on EVM chains at the same time. Those results will follow.

Where it could, the project ran its claims on the ledger instead of reading the specification, and it says which ones it only read. It keeps a public register of what it may claim and what it got wrong, and it filed eleven issues with the XRPLF repositories on GitHub. Five are resolved upstream so far.

It is a research project on a test network: not audited, not production-ready.

The write-up: https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
A read-only demo: https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app
The code and the claims register: https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions

XLS-96 is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, and its send proof builds on Tess Dore and Murat Cenk's compact sigma protocol.

Independent work; not affiliated with Ripple.

Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on Devnet, under XLS-96. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it to see exactly what it hides. The short answer: amounts, not relationships.
