## The blog post (figures are described by their alt text)

*Status, before anything else: a research project on the XRP Ledger's Devnet test
network. Not audited, not production-ready, and not safe to put value behind. Its
signer refuses every network but Devnet.*

> **Provenance.** Ids such as *E-58* below are rows in the project's claims register,
> [`CLAIMS.md`](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions/blob/main/CLAIMS.md).
> Each row says what supports it: a transaction run on Devnet, a line of source, or a
> document read on a stated date. If this post and a row ever disagree, trust the row.

---

Can a token move confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, under a standard called
XLS-96, and today only on Devnet. A new feature reaches the XRP Ledger as an
amendment, which a network's validators switch on. When I checked on 22 October
2026, XLS-96's amendment, `ConfidentialTransfer`, was enabled on Devnet, and
supported but not enabled on Mainnet and Testnet. That reading goes stale; the
repository has a script that takes a fresh one.

What XLS-96 hides is narrower than the word *confidential* suggests. It hides
balances, and the amounts of transfers between confidential balances. It does not
hide who pays whom, when, or how often. It does not hide amounts entering or
leaving confidential form. And it hides nothing from the token's issuer.

I set out to find exactly where that line falls by running transactions rather
than by reading the specification, and I started the same study on two ledgers at
once: the XRP Ledger, and EVM chains. This post is the XRP Ledger half. The EVM
results will follow in a separate post.

The XRP Ledger project is called W-CONF. Its code and claims register are public at
[github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions),
and a read-only demo is at
[xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app](https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app).

---

## What XLS-96 is, briefly

The XRP Ledger is public: anyone can read every account and every transaction.
Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its token types: an account issues a
token, and other accounts hold it. XLS-96, Confidential Transfers for MPTs, lets a
holder keep an MPT balance encrypted on that public ledger.

Each confidential balance is an ElGamal ciphertext, a public-key encryption of the
amount. A holder registers their own encryption key when they opt in. The ledger
still has to stop anyone spending more than they hold, so every transaction that
spends from a confidential balance carries zero-knowledge proofs, which validators
check without learning the amount.

A position moves through four transactions:

- **Convert** moves tokens from a public balance into the holder's confidential
  inbox. The amount is published.
- **Send** moves an amount from one confidential balance into another holder's
  inbox. The amount is hidden. The sender and receiver are not.
- **MergeInbox** moves the inbox into the balance the holder can spend. Arrivals
  wait in the inbox so that they cannot change a balance while a proof about it is
  being built, and they cannot be sent until they are merged.
- **ConvertBack** moves tokens back to a public balance. The amount is published.

Only Send hides an amount.

The specification, XLS-0096, is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo
Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, and is a final standard (E-1). The
compact sigma protocol, one of the zero-knowledge proofs behind a Send, is the work
of Tess Dore and Murat Cenk at RippleX Research. The reference cryptography is
[`XRPLF/mpt-crypto`](https://github.com/XRPLF/mpt-crypto). This project builds on
their work and claims none of it.

Upstream's code has had three outside reviews. None of them reviewed this project,
which has had no outside audit. Trail of Bits reviewed upstream's Confidential
Transfer implementation in April 2026; that report is the one I could read and
check my findings against, and a later revision of it could not be obtained. The
Sherlock XRP Ledger Attackathon was a contest that covered Confidential Transfers,
and its findings are not public. A Zellic scan of mpt-crypto is known to me only
through three identifiers an upstream issue cites. Of the three reviews, only Trail
of Bits' April report could be checked.

---

## What it hides, and what it does not

<figure>
  <img src="/images/posts/amounts-not-relationships/figure-1-where-the-line-falls.svg" alt="A token balance moves left to right. A public balance; an arrow labelled Convert, amount public, into a panel of confidential balances where holder A sends to holder B: the amount is hidden, the sender and receiver are public, and each balance is hidden unless it is visibly zero; an arrow labelled ConvertBack, amount public, out to a public balance. Below: public everywhere, who sends to whom, when and how often, and the total held in confidential form. The issuer reads every confidential balance, as does an auditor if the token names one, and no setting turns this off. A balance is visibly zero when it is new, when its inbox was just merged, or after a clawback.">
  <figcaption>Figure 1. Amounts are hidden inside confidential form and public at its edges. Who pays whom is public everywhere, and the issuer reads every balance.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Hidden from the public:** each holder's balance, and the amount of each Send.

**Public, always:**

- The sender and receiver of every transfer, and when it happened, so how often
  anyone transacts (P-4, P-11).
- Every amount converted in or out, each one separately.
- The token's total supply, and the total held in confidential form.
- That a balance is exactly zero, in three cases, below.

**Who can read every balance:** the issuer, always. XLS-96 keeps a second copy of
each confidential balance, encrypted to the issuer's key, and no setting turns it
off (P-9). An auditor can read them too, if the token names one, and only one is
supported (E-11). I ran this rather than inferring it. The holder, the issuer and
the auditor each decrypted the same balance, 500, and each read 475 after a
25-unit Send (E-58).

**Who can spend:** only whoever holds the holder's encryption secret, because a
Send's proof cannot be made without it (E-33). Where that secret is derived from
the account's master seed, as this project derives it, whoever holds the seed holds
the secret too. The issuer cannot spend a holder's balance. If the token allows
clawback, a setting that lets an issuer take tokens back, the issuer can destroy a
confidential balance, crediting no one, and this project's tokens allow clawback
(E-12). Unless the token's flags were made unchangeable when it was created, the
issuer can also turn on locking later and freeze balances. That second power I read
in rippled's source and did not run (E-290).

<figure>
  <img src="/images/posts/amounts-not-relationships/figure-2-who-can-read-who-can-spend.svg" alt="A table of who can see what. Columns: who pays whom and when; amounts converted in or out; a holder's balance; a Send's amount; can spend a balance. Anyone: yes, yes, only whether it is visibly zero, no, no. A holder: yes, yes, their own, their own, their own with both their keys. The issuer, highlighted: yes, yes, every one, every one, and no, though it can destroy one by clawback and may freeze one. An auditor, if the token names one: yes, yes, every one, every one, no.">
  <figcaption>Figure 2. Who can read what, and who can spend. A dashed cell is a partial yes.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Zero is sometimes visible.** XLS-96 writes a fixed encryption of zero, which
anyone can recompute from public inputs, in three places: a new confidential
balance, an inbox that a MergeInbox has just emptied, and a position clawed back.
So enrolment is publicly visible. The English documentation said this value could
not be told apart from other ciphertexts. I recomputed it from public inputs and
matched it byte for byte against live Devnet state (F-1, E-59), reported it, and the
English page was corrected. A balance spent down to zero holds a randomised
encryption of zero, and is not recognisable (E-211).

**The public numbers bound the hidden ones.** If a holder converts in 500, receives
nothing, and converts back 400, anyone can work out that the other 100 is either
still held or has left by confidential Send. No key is needed. I first wrote that
the 100 *"left by transfer"*. That overstated what an observer learns, and it is
recorded as a correction (R-7).

---

## No rotation, no recovery

A registered key can never be changed (E-9). XLS-96 has no key rotation and no key
recovery (P-10). If a holder loses their key, and any seed it could be re-derived
from, the balance cannot be spent. The only remedy is an issuer clawback, which
destroys the balance.

A draft standard, XLS-99, by Aanchal Malhotra and Yinyi Qian, proposes rotation for
holder, issuer and auditor keys, and recovery from key loss. When I checked, rippled
declared its amendment as not supported, in its development branch and in its
latest release candidate, and Mainnet, Testnet and Devnet did not know it (E-353).
So there is no rotation or recovery in XLS-96, or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet,
today.

---

## The example: a confidential receivables facility

To test the standard against something with stakes, I built the core of a
receivables facility. A bank pays a large buyer's suppliers early, against their
invoices. How much a supplier draws says a lot about its cash position, so these
amounts are commercially sensitive.

The bank issues a token. An ordinary XRPL account, which this project calls the
Dedicated Account, holds the float, the money the facility advances, and converts it
into confidential form once. Suppliers enrol, draw down by confidential Send, and
repay the same way. At the end, what is left of the float is retired in several
parts, called tranches, by ConvertBack. It ran on Devnet in 28 validated facility
transactions, besides setting up the token (E-146).

<figure>
  <img src="/images/posts/amounts-not-relationships/figure-3-the-facility.svg" alt="The facility's flow. The bank, which issues the token and reads every balance, funds the Dedicated Account with a public payment. The Dedicated Account makes one Convert of the whole float, amount public, so the float is confidential. Drawdowns and repayments are Sends between the float and suppliers A, B and C: amounts hidden, who and when public; each supplier's limit, draws and what it owes are hidden. Each supplier enrols with a small public payment and its own Convert, both amounts public. At the end, what is left of the float is retired in tranches, and each ConvertBack's amount is public. The public totals still bound the hidden amounts.">
  <figcaption>Figure 3. The facility as it ran on Devnet. The amounts that move between the float and the suppliers are hidden; the amounts at the edges are not.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Anyone can see** the size of the float, because converting it publishes the
amount. They can see which suppliers enrolled, who drew and repaid, on which days,
and how often. And they can see the size of every retirement tranche, because each
ConvertBack publishes its own amount (F-24). My own walkthrough first said a
ConvertBack published only *"the aggregate change"*. The validated transactions
showed each tranche in plaintext.

**Hidden from the public:** each supplier's limit, the size of each drawdown and
repayment, and what each supplier still owes. The bank, as issuer, sees all of it.
The public totals still bound these amounts, and in a small enough book they can pin
them exactly.

So it hides how much each supplier draws and owes. It does not hide who borrows,
when, how often, or the size of the whole. An early version of the design claimed
the facility *"shows nothing about which supplier drew how much"* (R-1). Which
supplier drew, and when, is public.

Two limits of that run. First, it read the ledger through a public Devnet node. The
design requires a node on the same machine, and a local Devnet node never finished
syncing on the hardware I had, so I accepted that as a named risk (E-148, E-151).
The run says nothing about that requirement. Second, one test driver played the
bank and every supplier and held every seed. The run shows that these transactions
are well formed and that rippled accepts them. It does not show how custody would
work.

---

## Reading the specification, and running it

Several of the things above I learned only by running them:

- That three different keys decrypt the same balance, through a change (E-58).
- That the encryption of zero matches a value anyone can recompute (F-1).
- That a balance spent to zero is not recognisable. My own observer page had
  labelled every ciphertext that was not the fixed zero as *"Non-zero"*, and a
  holder whose balance decrypted to 0 disproved it (E-211).
- That a failing transaction is not simply rejected. A `tec` result, one class of
  XRPL failure code, is still applied to the ledger: the fee is charged and the
  account's sequence number is used, though what the transaction asked for does not
  happen. The submission parameter `fail_hard` asks the node to discard it instead.
  I ran both on Devnet with a plain Payment that fails with `tecNO_AUTH`: the same
  signed bytes were applied without the flag, and discarded with it (E-149).

That last one matters more for confidential transactions than for plain ones,
because a `tec` keeps the transaction's fields, ciphertexts included. If a signer
reads a wrong destination key from a dishonest node, the amount is published
encrypted to that key for good, even though the transaction fails. That case I read
in rippled's source and did not run (F-23).

Running is not a substitute for reading what others have already found. Several
things I first recorded as findings turned out to be issues that Trail of Bits'
review had already found and Ripple had fixed.

---

## What the reviews caught

Design decisions and fixes went through rounds of adversarial review. These were
the project's own reviews: not outside audits, and not reviews by outside security
professionals. Each round gave its review passes deliberately different material,
so that their agreement would mean more than one reading copied three times. The
repository keeps more than sixty numbered review records, including the ones that
found me wrong. A few of the catches:

- **A secret not wiped from memory, behind a comment explaining why it could not
  be.** The comment said the secret's type belonged to an outside library. It was
  the project's own type, and one search of its file showed it had no wiping at all
  (E-200).
- **A design claim that four review passes independently ruled unsound.** I had
  written that the project's local read-only web viewer *"moves no trust
  boundary"*. It added no signing authority. But it re-served, to any local user,
  data the project protects with file permissions (E-230). That was the viewer that
  runs on the holder's machine, before the hosted demo existed; the demo serves only
  static files.
- **A release gate that passed a Content Security Policy every browser refused.**
  The gate hashed inline scripts over the file's bytes. Browsers hash the text they
  parse, which differs. Only loading the pages in a real browser showed it (E-334).
- **Fixes that did not fix.** In one review's second round, five of the first
  round's fixes had not discharged their findings. Only the review pass that ran
  each finding's own example against the fixed code found them (E-345).

The lesson I keep relearning: fixing something and describing the fix are two acts
that fail separately. A review that reads my summary of a finding will tick the
summary.

---

## Checks that catch a false sentence

The working rule is that a claim needs its evidence before it is written. The
claims register holds each established claim with what supports it, and twelve
standing prohibitions, P-1 to P-12, on what may not be claimed at all: that XLS-96
hides identities, that holders are private from the issuer, that it supports key
rotation, any benchmark without its hardware and method, and any claim that a
source does *not* say something without the search that would show otherwise.

Prose drifts anyway, so some of it is enforced by checks that run in CI. One fails
when a retracted phrase reappears without its correction. One fails when a note
meant for upstream says something is missing from a source and does not record the
search that found it missing. One keeps the register's derived indexes in step with
it.

They do not catch everything. The register keeps nine correction records, R-1 to
R-9. Most withdraw or narrow something this project claimed; one records a
retraction that was itself reversed. R-8 said every confidential transaction needs
both of a holder's keys, when a MergeInbox needs only the account key; it was on the
public demo until a review pass found it repeated in a diagram caption. R-9 came
from reviewing this post. The README and the demo summarised the facility as hiding
*"the shape of the book, not its size"*, and a reader new to the project took
*shape* to mean who borrows and when, which is public. That sentence is replaced
everywhere, and a check now refuses it.

At one point the register still listed as open four filings that upstream had
already fixed (E-316). Nothing re-checked them until I surveyed every filing at
source. That survey now runs before anything I publish about them, this post
included.

---

## What went upstream

This project has filed eleven issues in four XRPLF repositories. Their state when I
checked, read at source (E-353):

- **Four resolved.** Three issues against the XLS-0096 text were resolved in the
  merged standard. The documentation's sentence calling the zero value
  indistinguishable was corrected on the English page. The Japanese translation was
  made from the text before the fix, and still carries it.
- **The mpt-crypto build.** Its lockfile pinned an OpenSSL revision that the
  documented package remote did not serve. Fixed on mpt-crypto's main branch, not
  yet in a release. I re-ran the check against the merged commit, and it resolves.
- **The fixed zero, from JavaScript.** mpt-crypto's WASM and npm packages did not
  expose the function that computes the fixed encryption of zero, which is the check
  an outside observer most needs. A maintainer agreed and a pull request is approved
  and not merged. I have offered to write the JavaScript wrapper once it is
  released.
- **Three filed most recently, against mpt-crypto, with no reply yet:** an
  ambiguity in what the compact sigma paper's nonce input covers; a WASM build
  script that fails outside its pinned toolchain; and a proof-size total in the
  paper that assumes a ciphertext component is sent once, where rippled and XLS-0096
  send it per recipient.
- **A question to XRPL-Standards**, whether a confidential balance is meant to stay
  invisible to the accounting of the ledger's vaults (XLS-65), which pool one asset
  and issue shares against it, has had no reply in nearly two months.
- **A filing to rippled that listed only things done well** was closed without
  comment the day it was filed, so its reason is not known. It also fit neither of
  that repository's two issue templates, and the project's filing rules now forbid a
  positives-only filing to a bug tracker.

I do not call any of these new, or unreported. Of the three outside reviews of
upstream's code, I could check my findings against one.

---

## What it does not show

- **No run against a local node.** Every Devnet read went to the public cluster
  (E-151).
- **Custody is accepted, not solved.** The issuer can erase or freeze the facility's
  float. The Dedicated Account's key both moves the float and decrypts every amount
  sent to or from it, so those two powers cannot be held apart (E-266).
- **The key derivation is unpublished.** It is specified in this repository only, so
  a holder with their master seed but not this repository cannot reconstruct their
  key. Treat it as lock-in until it is published.
- **A hostile process running as the same user** can read the encryption secret out
  of memory.

---

## Try it

The demo is static pages built from one snapshot of Devnet. It signs nothing and
holds no keys. It shows what an observer reads of four test accounts, including
which balances are visibly zero; which encrypted copies the issuer can read, without
publishing the figures; and what each kind of key can do. It does not show the
facility, whose record is in the repository.

To transact, you run the signer yourself, on your own machine. The README explains
how to build it and run the local version of the site. It does not yet walk through
creating a holder profile and funded Devnet accounts, which a transaction needs.

The repository has the Rust signer, the TypeScript facility, the read-only web
viewer, the claims register and the review records, under Apache-2.0.

---

## What to take from it

- **XLS-96 hides amounts, not relationships.** Balances and Send amounts are
  hidden from the public. Who pays whom, when and how often is not.
- **The edges are public.** Every Convert and ConvertBack publishes its amount, and
  the totals bound what is hidden.
- **The issuer sees everything.** It reads every balance, can destroy one by
  clawback, and may be able to freeze one.
- **Keys are for life.** No rotation and no recovery, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet,
  Testnet or Devnet today. XLS-99 is a draft that would add both.
- **Running it found things reading did not**, and reading what others had already
  found saved me from calling their findings mine.

**Next:** the same study on EVM chains.

If something in this is wrong, please tell me, by an issue on the repository. The
register has a section for corrections, and it has nine entries.

FIGURE 1 ("Only a Send hides its amount. Who pays whom is always public.")
1. Says: tokens move from an ordinary public balance into a confidential pool (Convert), can be sent between holders with the amount hidden (Send), and move back out (ConvertBack). Convert and ConvertBack amounts are public. Observers always see sender, receiver, timing and the total confidential; the issuer (and an auditor, if named) can read every confidential balance. I understood it, though "visibly zero" is only explained in the footnote.
2. Arrows: "Convert" (left box to the confidential box) = holder moves a public holding in; "amount public" under it is clear. "Send" holder A to holder B = A pays B, amount hidden; clear. "ConvertBack" = confidential to public holding; clear. Issue: the two outer boxes are both titled "A public balance", so it can read as one balance or as two unrelated ones. The Convert and ConvertBack arrows enter and leave the big box's edge, not holder A / holder B specifically, so it is unclear whose balance moves. Nothing is mislabelled by grouping, but the "PUBLIC EVERYWHERE" and "THE ISSUER READS..." panels sit below with no link to the diagram, which is fine.
3. Colour: the dark thick border/left bar and dark Send arrow on the confidential box read as "the protected zone". That implies safe/private, which the box's own text only partly supports. The small grey "amount public" labels are low emphasis, so the public parts read as minor while the dark parts draw the eye.
4. Stronger than it should: the dark framing around "CONFIDENTIAL BALANCES" plus "amount hidden" visually promises privacy, while the issuer-reads caveat is in a plain grey box at the bottom. "each balance hidden, unless visibly zero" says "hidden" with no "from whom"; the issuer panel fixes this but is far from it. "No setting turns this off." is good and clear.
5. Legibility: fine. The grey "amount public" and "sender and receiver public" text is small and light but readable. The footnote is italic and light grey.
6. Fixes: change "each balance hidden, unless visibly zero" to "each balance hidden from the public, unless visibly zero". Change "amount hidden" to "amount hidden from observers". Rename the right box "A public balance" to "A public balance again" (as Figure 3 does) or add "(holder's)" to both. Define "visibly zero" in the footnote itself or inline.

FIGURE 2 ("The issuer reads every balance. Only the holder's keys can spend one.")
1. Says: a matrix of four parties (anyone, a holder, the issuer, an auditor if named) against five things. Everyone sees who pays whom and conversion amounts. Only holders (their own) and the issuer/auditor (every one) can read balances and Send amounts. Only a holder, with both keys, can spend; the issuer cannot spend but can destroy one by clawback or may freeze one.
2. Arrows: none. Grouping: row order puts "The issuer" accent-marked between "A holder" and "An auditor", which is fine. The auditor row looks like the issuer row without the emphasis, which is accurate.
3. Colour: dashed borders mean "partial yes" (the footer says so). The dark outline on the issuer's two "every one" cells and the dark bar on the issuer row mean "this is the point". Grey fill means "no". Possible mis-read: dashed for "their own" under a holder reads as "less certain/partial" when it is actually a full yes to their own data. Grey "no" cells read as "greyed out/disabled" rather than a positive guarantee, which is slightly weak for the headline "no" on Anyone/Can spend.

Stronger than it should: the "no" in "Can spend a balance" for the issuer and auditor is stated flatly, and the "no; can destroy one by clawback, may freeze one" is small grey text that could be skimmed past. FIGURE 3 ("It hides how much each supplier draws and owes, not who or when.")

75:| E-34 | **Nonce reuse in a compact-form sigma proof leaks `sk_A`, and is undetectable from the proofs.** Compact form transmits `(e, z…)` not the commitments, so reused nonces yield proofs that verify normally while allowing an observer holding both to extract the witness. ⚠ **That mitigation line is FALSE and was falsified by two independent cryptography reviewers on 2026-08-17 (REVIEW-005a, REVIEW-005b, adjudicated in REVIEW-005c §1).** `statement` does not include `TransactionContextID` as the paper defines it, while the Fiat–Shamir challenge does — so an ordinary resubmission at a changed sequence or `CB_S_Version`, with cached ciphertexts, yields two proofs sharing first-round commitments under distinct challenges. The C reduction is also checked against `scalar::reduce_wide` — a second implementation written in Rust from REVIEW-010's prose — over five inputs including `n` itself | A, executed |
133:| E-82 | **The Rust FFI struct layouts and by-value ABI are checked against the vendored header by the C compiler, not by hand.** `tests/prover_ffi.rs` compiles a probe against `include/utility/mpt_utility.h` and compares its `sizeof`/`offsetof` for `mpt_confidential_participant` and `mpt_pedersen_proof_params` against Rust's. Separately, `account_id` and `mpt_issuance_id` are passed **by value** across the boundary, and a Rust/C ABI disagreement there would be **invisible end-to-end** — our prover and our verifier would both use the same wrong context — so the context hashes a Rust caller computes are compared against `mptool`'s for identical inputs, as are `EncZero` and ElGamal encryption | **Executed 2026-08-18.** Hand-written expected sizes would have been exactly the fabricated-constant defect of E-75; the C compiler is the independent tool | A, executed |
134:| E-83 | **XRPL serialisation and signing are implemented in the signer and pinned byte-for-byte against three implementations this project did not write.** `signer/src/xrpl.rs` — canonical field ordering, VL prefixes, `STX\0` signing serialisation, `SHA512Half`, base58check, family-seed derivation for **both secp256k1 and ed25519**, and the transaction hash. `tests/xrpl_vectors.rs` checks all of it against vectors generated by `ripple-binary-codec@2.9.0`, `ripple-keypairs@2.0.0` and `ripple-address-codec@5.0.1`, with the generator committed at `tools/spike-step3-2026-08-18/xrpl-vectors.ts` under **P-8**. ⚠ **The two algorithms sign different things** — secp256k1 signs `SHA512Half(message)`, ed25519 signs the message — and both are pinned rather than reasoned about. ed25519 is not optional: every account in this project's Devnet state has an `sEd…` seed | **Executed 2026-08-18.** 9 vector tests. `txn::serialize`'s length-framed placeholder and its `WCONF-SKEL-TXN-v1` magic are **gone** | A, executed |
135:| E-84 | **A `ConfidentialMPTSend` built, proved and signed entirely by `signer/` was accepted on Devnet.** `tesSUCCESS`, validated, `9170912934A842CE90494E66485ADC82739B2276ECD48E2900A1F62A164F9DB0` — 1428 bytes, 946-byte `ZKProof`. The driver `tools/spike-step3-2026-08-18/devnet-signer-send.ts` reads public ledger state, hands the signer a profile, asks over a Unix socket and submits the blob; **it signs nothing and holds no proof**. The hash the signer computed matched the node's exactly, which is what says the serialisation is canonical rather than merely accepted. The request carried a deliberately false `claimed` block and the confirmation showed the real fields | **Executed 2026-08-18**, network_id 2, rippled 3.3.0. ⚠ **`tesSUCCESS` is not a confidentiality claim.** Amounts are hidden; identities, counterparties, timing and frequency are not, and the issuer decrypts everything (P-4, P-9, P-11) | A, executed |
136:| E-85 | **E-76 is closed: `observer-harness.ts --assert-no-r-reuse` has now been run against transactions this project's own code produced, and it passes.** Architecture §6 step 4's named falsifier had never fired, because nothing signed. It could not be run against the 2026-08-17 holder either — **that account's history contains E-63's deliberately broken Sends**, and the assertion fires on them correctly whatever this signer does. So `tools/spike-step3-2026-08-18/devnet-clean-account.ts` built a **clean** holder, `rnU7af8QRAgE2Qp7qeAYJLgeMmmTcbvX81`, whose every confidential transaction — one Convert and two Sends — came from `signer/`. **ASSERTION PASSED: no ElGamal randomness reuse across 7 transactions**, exit 0 | **Executed 2026-08-18.** The contaminated-account run is recorded too: it exits 1 and names exactly the two E-63 hashes, which is the falsifier working. Two Sends rather than one, because "no reuse" across a single transaction is vacuous | A, executed |
137:| E-86 | **The randomness ledger's records are checkable against the public ledger, and were checked.** `r_entry` commits to `compressed(r·G)` and `C₁ = r·G` is on the wire, so anyone holding `k_local` can take transactions off the chain and confirm the randomness they published is the randomness the signer recorded. `signer/src/bin/store-check.rs` does exactly that: it verifies the whole hash chain, header MAC and audit log on open, then looks up each `C₁`. Run against the three `C₁` values pulled from Devnet for E-85's account: **all three RECORDED, committed**, exit 0 | **Executed 2026-08-18.** Verified in the other direction too — E-63's reused `C₁` from the *other* account reports `*** NOT IN THE LEDGER ***`, exit 1. The store held **12 records** for three signings, which is reserve+commit for `r` and `ρ` each time | A, executed |
138:| E-87 | ⚠ **A real defect in the signing path was found by a test, not by review, and it would have been rejected by every validator.** `SigningPubKey` is a **signing field**, and the first draft of `session::prove_confirm_and_sign` added it *after* computing the digest — so the signature covered a serialisation the blob did not contain. Found by `tests/signing_path.rs::the_signature_verifies_over_the_blob_that_carries_it`, which verifies the signature against the bytes **in the returned blob** rather than against the bytes the function happened to hold. A test that re-used the signer's own serialisation would have passed | **Executed 2026-08-18.** Recorded because the test's design is the whole reason it caught anything, and a weaker version of the same test was the obvious thing to write | A |
139:| E-88 | ⚠ **`session.rs` now calls `store` and `randomness` on the signing path, in the order the rulings require, and there are tests that fail if it does not.** Both `REVIEW-014` legs recorded the gap. `tests/signing_path.rs`: a signing appends **four** records (reserve and commit for `r` and `ρ`); the identifier recorded is the one for the `C₁` the transaction published; **a declined confirmation burns rather than clears** (A7), and so does a refusal that happens after the reservation; five consecutive signings never share a `C₁`; two attempts in a **byte-identical context** still produce different randomness, which is A9's corrected claim that fresh entropy — not the store — is the primary defence | **Executed 2026-08-18.** 9 tests. The entropy-failure path is exercised through a one-shot hook compiled **only** under the non-default `test-support` feature, because inducing a real `/dev/urandom` failure is not something a test can do and the claim *"entropy failure refuses to sign"* needs a falsifier | A, executed |
140:| E-89 | **Step 3 was adversarially reviewed and the review found a defect that would have broken every Send on an auditor-enabled issuance.** `REVIEW-015`, two independent legs against the committed diff of `16e2e58` — Gemini via `agy` (diff only) and Codex (repository access), neither shown the other's output. **Both found the same defect independently**, which is the strongest signal available: `prover::prepare_send` builds a **four-participant** proof when an `AuditorEncryptionKey` is configured, and `WireFields::Send` had no `AuditorEncryptedAmount`, so the transaction carried three ciphertexts against a four-participant proof. **Invisible on Devnet** because the test issuance has no auditor, and invisible in tests because no fixture had one. Both legs also found that `Convert` skipped the issuance check `Send` performs | **Fixed 2026-08-18**, with `fixture_with_auditor` and a test that decrypts the auditor's ciphertext under the auditor's own key. ⚠ **The field is `nth=43`.** One leg proposed 42, which is `AuditorEncryptedBalance` — a different field on a different object — so the code was checked against `ripple-binary-codec`'s definitions rather than taken. **A review finding is evidence, not an instruction** | A, executed |
141:| E-90 | **The review found that validation ran AFTER the randomness reservation, and that a test had codified it as intended.** A request that was always going to be refused — wrong issuance, over the balance, a destination with no registered encryption key — drew entropy, derived `r` and `ρ`, and burned two **append-only** identifiers before being refused. A hostile local process, which the issue #1 ruling puts in scope, could grow the ledger without ever reaching a human. **`session::preflight` now runs before any entropy is drawn**, and `a_request_refusable_before_signing_never_touches_the_randomness_ledger` asserts the ledger is untouched across four refusal shapes | **Fixed 2026-08-18.** ⚠ **The old test asserted the defect.** `a_refusal_after_reserving_still_burns_the_reservation` used an over-spend — refusable before any randomness exists — and asserted four records were burned, which made the wrong order look deliberate. It is replaced, and the replacement says so. A7's burn property is still covered on the **declined-confirmation** path, which genuinely happens after the reservation | A, executed |
142:| E-91 | **`ParsedTransaction::parse` ignored fields it did not recognise, while its own doc comment claimed it refused them — and one such field would have put a plaintext amount on the confirmation screen.** `MPTAmount` on a `ConfidentialMPTSend` parsed cleanly and set `AmountView::Public`, so the confirmation would have rendered *"1 (PUBLIC — in the clear on the wire)"* for a ciphertext encrypting something else entirely. That is the value-shaped-confirmation failure REVIEW-003b exists to prevent, reintroduced through a field-presence check. **Fixed with a per-transaction-type allowlist**, and the amount view is now derived from the **transaction type** rather than from which fields happen to be present, so a Send can never render a plaintext number | **Fixed 2026-08-18.** Found by both legs, from different directions: one as "the doc comment is false", one as "this specific field defeats the confirmation". The same allowlist also refuses `NetworkID`, which Devnet rejects outright (F-21) | A, executed |
143:| E-92 | ⚠ **The step 3 falsifier could be pointed at the wrong binary, and every test would still have passed.** `tests/prover_pristine.rs` resolved the "pristine upstream verifier" from `WCONF_MPTOOL_PRISTINE` or a default path and **never checked what it got**. Aimed at the *patched* `mptool`, all seven tests pass — including the corrupted-proof test, which only shows the verifier is not a rubber stamp — while the claim the milestone rests on is no longer being tested at all. **Fixed:** the binary's symbol table is checked for `secp256k1_mpt_scalar_reduce64`, which exists only in the W-CONF patch, and a `#[should_panic]` test aims the check at the patched binary to prove it can fire | **Fixed 2026-08-18.** Found by leg B. **This is the round's most valuable finding** and it is a pure test-quality defect: no shipped code was wrong, and the evidence for the whole vendoring argument was resting on a path string | A, executed |
144:| E-93 | **Two round-one findings were WRONG, and both are now pinned by tests rather than by a disposition note.** (1) A leg ruled that a **zero** XRP drops Amount must serialise as eight zero bytes and that setting bit 62 is non-canonical. It is not: `ripple-binary-codec` encodes `Fee: "0"` as `4000000000000000`, positive bit set, exactly as for any other value. (2) A leg ruled that `b58_encode`'s trailing cleanup strips legitimate payload digits equal to the zero character, corrupting addresses. It cannot: the most significant base-58 digit of a non-zero value is never zero, because a non-zero top digit forces a carry of at least 4 on every subsequent byte, so the cleanup can only fire on an all-zero payload — where it is correct | **Refuted 2026-08-18, then tested anyway.** The second refutation is a proof sketch, and a proof sketch is the kind of thing that is wrong one time in twenty, so it is backed by a brute-force round trip over 2023 payloads including every count of leading zero bytes. **A refutation that lives only in a disposition note is a finding somebody re-raises next round**, and the second time nobody re-derives the argument | A, executed |
145:| E-94 | **Round two reviewed the FIXES and found a defect one of them introduced, a test that passed for the wrong reason, and four overclaims.** `REVIEW-015d`/`e`. (a) The round-one allowlist fix permitted `AuditorEncryptedAmount` on `Convert` while the signer never emitted it there — and a leg recommended **removing** it. **The spec says the opposite:** XLS-0096 §7.2 makes it *required* when the issuance has an auditor key, §7.3.2 item 1 makes its absence `tecNO_PERMISSION`. So the permissiveness was real and its cause was the reverse of the diagnosis: the signer was **missing the field on Convert too**, the same defect one transaction type over. (b) `an_auditor_enabled_issuance…` asserted that the blob **re-parsed** under a comment claiming the confirmation disclosed the auditor; nothing rendered it and `ParsedTransaction` had no such field. (c) Four sentences overstated — *"really is the pristine one"*, *"everything checkable, before any entropy"*, *"burns them on any refusal"*, and the auditor comment | **Fixed 2026-08-18.** 118 tests. **Two fixes spot-checked by reverting them and confirming the tests fail.** ⚠ **The second time in this project a leg's diagnosis was right and its remedy backwards** (`REVIEW-014c` records the first). The rule: check a recommendation against the primary source before applying it, especially when applying is cheaper than checking | A, executed |
146:| E-95 | **Reading the spec to settle a review question found a defect neither review round did.** XLS-0096 §7.2: `HolderEncryptionKey` is **required when initialising and forbidden once registered** (`tecDUPLICATE`, §7.3.2 item 3), and `ZKProof` is required exactly when it is present and *"MUST be absent"* when it is not. **The signer always emitted both**, so it could register a holder once and would have failed every `ConfidentialMPTConvert` after that. `holder_key_registered` is now part of the holder profile and both branches are executed on Devnet: the initialising Convert and a second Convert on the same already-registered account, both `tesSUCCESS` | **Executed 2026-08-18** on `rnU7af8QRAgE2Qp7qeAYJLgeMmmTcbvX81`. ⚠ **The failure mode is asserted from the spec, not observed** — `tecDUPLICATE` is what §7.3.2 item 3 says a re-registration returns; this project did not spend a transaction proving it. Say "the spec says", not "we saw" | A, executed |
147:| E-96 | **A third review round was run against this project's own two-round rule, and it found a defect neither earlier round could have.** `CLAUDE.md` says a third round *"reviews the fixes to the fixes; that is where it stops paying."* It was run anyway, scoped to one argument: **round two's fixes changed `Convert`'s wire format on the strength of the adjudicator's own reading of XLS-0096 §7.2, and no second reader had seen them.** The finding: `ParsedTransaction::parse` applied `Convert`'s `HolderEncryptionKey`/`ZKProof` pairing rule to **`ConvertBack`** via a `_` wildcard. **Reading §10.3 to settle it showed the problem was three-fold** — ConvertBack has a *required* 816-byte `ZKProof`, **no `HolderEncryptionKey` field at all**, and a *required* `BalanceCommitment` the shared allowlist omitted. A valid ConvertBack would have been **rejected twice over** and an invalid one accepted | **Fixed 2026-08-19** by refusing `ConvertBack` in `parse` rather than implementing a field set nothing has exercised, with a test, and by striking the doc comment that claimed coverage. Three more: a defaulted `holder_key_registered` that would walk a registered holder into `tecDUPLICATE`; an auditor test that proved decryptability but **not** the shared-`C₁` invariant it claimed; and a README that compressed a *conditional* spec requirement into an unconditional one. **121 tests.** ⚠ **This does not overturn the two-round rule.** It says the rule counts rounds of review, and a fix that introduces new protocol-facing behaviour is a new thing to review | A, executed |
148:| E-97 | ⚠ **IT HAPPENED AGAIN on 2026-08-25, mid-session, and the window turned out to be DAYS → E-133.** ⚠ **The entire executable evidence base lived in `/tmp` and `/tmp` was cleaned mid-session, and only half of it was reproducible.** On 2026-08-19 the platform removed `/tmp/wconf`, holding the vendored patched `mpt-crypto`, the built libraries, both `mptool` binaries, the XLS-0096 text and `state.json` with the Devnet account seeds, issuance ID and ElGamal secrets. The signer stopped building — and `build.rs` said exactly why and named the two commands to fix it, which is the one part of this that worked as designed. **Reproducible:** the vendored tree, from `git clone` at the pin plus the **committed** patch, with `vendor-verify.sh` passing on the rebuild — **this is issue #2 path A's central argument paying off, tested by accident**; secp256k1; both libraries; and the XLS-0096 text, re-fetched from `XRPLF/XRPL-Standards` rather than from a copy. **NOT reproducible: `state.json`.** The Devnet accounts and every recorded transaction hash remain verifiable by anyone; what is lost is the ability to drive those accounts | **Observed 2026-08-19.** `E-70` was independently re-confirmed on the fresh clone — `git tag --points-at HEAD` on `85dbac7` returns `1.0.4`. **The distinction that held is the one worth keeping: evidence recorded as transaction hashes survived; a harness that could re-run it did not.** Throwaway keys are the right call; a throwaway key that cannot be regenerated makes a harness single-use, and nothing warned about it | A |
149:| E-98 | ⚠ **The test suite was FLAKY and several "all passing" reports were true but lucky.** The entropy-failure hook added in step 3 — `store::fail_next_entropy_draw_for_test`, written specifically to make the claim *"entropy failure refuses to sign"* falsifiable — set a **process-global** `AtomicBool`. `cargo test` runs a binary's tests on **parallel threads**, so the induced failure landed in whichever test drew entropy next rather than the one that asked for it. Measured: **2 failing runs in 12** with the global flag, **0 in 12** after making it `thread_local!`, and **0 in 6** full-suite runs. Verified in both directions by restoring the old code and re-running | **Found and fixed 2026-08-19**, while re-verifying after round three. ⚠ **This retroactively weakens every earlier "N tests, all passing" statement in this milestone** — they were accurate reports of runs that happened to be green, not evidence that the suite was sound. **The hook written to make a claim falsifiable was itself unsound**, which is the sharpest form of this project's recurring lesson. The shared C `secp256k1` context was checked for the same class of defect and is safe: a C++11 function-local static, thread-safe on first init, with `secp256k1_context_randomize` called exactly once inside it | A, executed |
150:| E-99 | ⚠ **`tools/rebuild-env.sh` restored an environment that could not rebuild a Devnet chain, and looked complete doing it.** `build.sh` produces `mptool-patched`, `mptool-pristine` and `mptool-deterministic`; the plain `/tmp/wconf/mptool` that the 2026-08-17 spike built is produced by **nothing**, and five tools still call it by that name — `convert.ts`, `send.ts`, `wasm-test.ts`, `npm-package-test.ts` and `reuse-r-setup.ts`. 151:| E-100 | **Architecture §6 step 2 is built: the signer reads the ledger itself, and the profile file no longer carries any ledger state.** `signer/src/ledger.rs` speaks XRPL JSON-RPC over TLS, **refuses any `network_id` but 2 before it reads anything else**, and assembles one snapshot at **one pinned numeric ledger index** — `account_info` for `Sequence` and issue #11's three account conditions, `ledger_entry mptoken` for `ConfidentialBalanceSpending`, `ConfidentialBalanceVersion` and `HolderEncryptionKey`, `ledger_entry mpt_issuance` for `IssuerEncryptionKey` and `AuditorEncryptionKey`, and the destination's own `MPToken` for its `HolderEncryptionKey`. 152:| E-101 | **A `ConfidentialMPTSend` built, proved and signed entirely by `signer/` *from ledger state the signer read for itself* was accepted on Devnet.** `tesSUCCESS`, validated, `C63CDCB41183DF55A1CBE9B955AD5EB5C7FE037037AC87EDE31DC4799C5C0EDE`, and the hash the signer computed matched the node's exactly. 153:| E-102 | **A stale ledger read is now *detected*, not merely bounded — the signer re-reads after the human confirms and refuses if anything the transaction binds to moved.** Architecture §6 step 2's second falsifier is *"a stale read is indistinguishable from a fresh one"*, and bounding the age of a read does not answer it: the window is the confirmation itself, which a human can hold open for minutes while `Sequence` and `ConfidentialBalanceVersion` move. `LedgerSnapshot::binding_differs` compares only the fields a transaction binds to, so an ordinary ledger close does not fire it | **2026-08-19.** Four tests drive it, and the **control** — a ledger that merely advances 7 ledgers during the confirmation still signs — is what stops the other three being vacuous. 154:| E-103 | **Two `"validated"` reads seconds apart land in different ledgers, so a snapshot assembled from them is a state that never existed.** Observed live on 2026-08-19: `account_objects` answered at ledger 4596692 and `account_info` at 4596693, issued back to back — the public Devnet endpoint is a **cluster**, and consecutive requests reached hosts `FUSS` and `JUTE`. 155:| E-104 | **Reading the balance from the ledger made the search bound load-bearing in a second place, and made one earlier test's scenario unreachable.** `amount_search_to` bounded only the confirmation's discrete-log search while the balance was a number in a file. It now also bounds the **balance**, and a Send enforces `amount <= balance`, so on the `prepare` path `amount <= balance <= amount_search_to` — the confirmation's `*** COULD NOT BE READ ***` branch **cannot be reached through `prepare` any more**. The refusal moved earlier and is stronger (`REFUSED_BALANCE_UNREADABLE`, before any entropy is drawn), but *unreachable from one caller* is not *dead*: the branch is still tested, on a real transaction this signer built, re-parsed with a bound too small to read it, with a control at a bound that can | **2026-08-19.** ⚠ Recorded because deleting the old test would have removed the only check that `render` never guesses, and keeping it unchanged would have made it assert nothing | A, executed |
188:## Phase 3 — the two posts
     1	---
     2	layout: post
     3	title: "Amounts, not relationships: what confidential transfers on the XRP Ledger hide"
     4	excerpt: "XLS-96 lets a token holder keep balances encrypted on the public XRP Ledger. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it on Devnet to see exactly where the line falls. It hides how much moves inside confidential form. It does not hide who pays whom, when, the amounts at the edges, or anything from the issuer."

    15	
    16	*Status, before anything else: a research project on the XRP Ledger's Devnet test
    17	network. Not audited, not production-ready, and not safe to put value behind. Its
    18	signer refuses every network but Devnet.*
    19	
    20	> **How to read the ids.** Ids in parentheses, such as *(E-58)*, point to rows in the
    21	> project's claims register,
    22	> [`CLAIMS.md`](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions/blob/main/CLAIMS.md).
    23	> You can read the post without them. They are there so that you can check it. The
    24	> letter says what kind of row it is:
    25	>
    26	> - **E**, established: a claim, with what supports it. That is a transaction run on
    27	>   Devnet, a line of source code, or a document read on a stated date.
    28	> - **F**, a finding: a verified problem, in upstream's standard, code or
    29	>   documentation, or in this project's own.
    30	> - **P**, a prohibition: something this project must never claim, and why.
    31	> - **R**, a correction: something this project said, and later withdrew or narrowed.
    32	> - **B**, pending: something asserted that the evidence does not yet support.
    33	>
    34	> To find a row, open the register, use your browser's find for the id, such as
    35	> `E-58`, and look for it in the first column of a table. Other rows that cite it
    36	> will match too. To browse by subject instead, the register has
    37	> [topic pages](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions/blob/main/docs/claims/by-topic/README.md).
    38	> If this post and a row ever disagree, trust the row.
    39	
    40	---
    41	
    42	Can a token move confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, under a standard called
    43	XLS-96, and today only on Devnet. A new feature reaches the XRP Ledger as an
    44	amendment, which a network's validators switch on. When I checked on 22 October
    45	2026, XLS-96's amendment, `ConfidentialTransfer`, was enabled on Devnet, and
    46	supported but not enabled on Mainnet and Testnet. That reading goes stale; the
    47	repository has a script that takes a fresh one.
    48	
    49	What XLS-96 hides is narrower than the word *confidential* suggests. It hides
    50	balances, and the amounts of transfers between confidential balances. It does not
    51	hide who pays whom, when, or how often. It does not hide amounts entering or
    52	leaving confidential form. And it hides nothing from the token's issuer.
    53	
    54	I set out to find exactly where that line falls by running transactions rather
    55	than by reading the specification, and I started the same study on two ledgers at
    56	once: the XRP Ledger, and EVM chains. This post is the XRP Ledger half. The EVM
    57	results will follow in a separate post.
    58	
    59	The XRP Ledger project is called W-CONF. Its code and claims register are public at
    60	[github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions](https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions),
    61	and a read-only demo is at
    62	[xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app](https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app).
    63	
    64	---
    65	
    66	## Why it matters: the business case
    67	
    68	Large buyers often pay their suppliers' invoices weeks or months after delivery. A
    69	supplier that needs the cash sooner can draw it from a bank against those invoices,
    70	and repay when the buyer pays. That is receivables finance, and its numbers are
    71	sensitive in a specific way:
    72	
    73	- **A supplier's drawings show its cash position.** One that draws more, or more
    74	  often, is short of cash. Published, that tells its competitors, its customers and
    75	  its other lenders.
    76	- **The bank's limits and balances are its book.** What it has lent each supplier,
    77	  and against what limit, is its exposure, and it does not publish that.
    78	- **The suppliers should not see each other.** A supplier that could read another's
    79	  limit and drawings would learn its position and what the bank granted it.
    80	
    81	Why put this on a shared ledger at all? Off one, the same facility lives in several
    82	records, the bank's and each supplier's, which have to be reconciled. The usual case for a
    83	shared ledger is one record that the bank, the suppliers and a supervisor all read,
    84	with the money moving on that record. This post does not test that case. It tests
    85	whether the privacy the business needs survives the move.
    86	
    87	That is the dilemma. On a public ledger in plaintext, every drawing is published, and
    88	with it each supplier's cash position. On a private ledger, much of what a shared
    89	record was for is given up. Confidential transfers are an attempt at the middle:
    90	amounts encrypted on a public ledger, and readable by the parties who answer for the
    91	book.
    92	
    93	So a business would ask concrete questions before using them:
    94	
    95	1. Can the public see what each supplier draws and owes?
    96	2. Can the public see who draws, and when?
    97	3. Can one supplier see another's position?
    98	4. Can the bank see every position? It lends the money, so it must.
    99	5. Can an auditor or supervisor see them too?
   100	6. What happens if someone loses a key?
   101	7. What can the bank do to a supplier's balance without the supplier?
   102	
   103	The facility below answers them as it ran on Devnet.
   104	
   105	---
   106	
   107	## What XLS-96 is, briefly
   108	
   109	The XRP Ledger is public: anyone can read every account and every transaction.
   110	Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its token types: an account issues a
   111	token, and other accounts hold it. XLS-96, Confidential Transfers for MPTs, lets a
   112	holder keep an MPT balance encrypted on that public ledger.
   113	
   114	Each confidential balance is an ElGamal ciphertext, a public-key encryption of the
   115	amount. A holder registers their own encryption key when they opt in. The ledger
   116	still has to stop anyone spending more than they hold, so every transaction that
   117	spends from a confidential balance carries zero-knowledge proofs, which validators
   118	check without learning the amount.
   119	
   120	A position moves through four transactions:
   121	
   122	- **Convert** moves tokens from a public balance into the holder's confidential
   123	  inbox. The amount is published.
   124	- **Send** moves an amount from one confidential balance into another holder's
   125	  inbox. The amount is hidden. The sender and receiver are not.
   126	- **MergeInbox** moves the inbox into the balance the holder can spend. Arrivals
   127	  wait in the inbox so that they cannot change a balance while a proof about it is
   128	  being built, and they cannot be sent until they are merged.
   129	- **ConvertBack** moves tokens back to a public balance. The amount is published.
   130	
   131	Only Send hides an amount.
   132	
   133	The specification, XLS-0096, is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo
   134	Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian, and is a final standard (E-1). The
   135	compact sigma protocol, one of the zero-knowledge proofs behind a Send, is the work
   136	of Tess Dore and Murat Cenk at RippleX Research. The reference cryptography is
   137	[`XRPLF/mpt-crypto`](https://github.com/XRPLF/mpt-crypto). This project builds on
   138	their work and claims none of it.
   139	
   140	Upstream's code has had three outside reviews. None of them reviewed this project,
   141	which has had no outside audit. Trail of Bits reviewed upstream's Confidential
   142	Transfer implementation in April 2026; that report is the one I could read and
   143	check my findings against, and a later revision of it could not be obtained. The
   144	Sherlock XRP Ledger Attackathon was a contest that covered Confidential Transfers,
   145	and its findings are not public. A Zellic scan of mpt-crypto is known to me only
   146	through three identifiers an upstream issue cites. Of the three reviews, only Trail
   147	of Bits' April report could be checked.
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## What it hides, and what it does not
   152	
   153	<figure>
   154	  <img src="/images/posts/amounts-not-relationships/figure-1-where-the-line-falls.svg" alt="A token balance moves left to right. Holder A's public balance; an arrow labelled Convert, amount public, into a panel of confidential balances where holder A sends to holder B: the amount is hidden from the public, the sender and receiver are public, and each balance is hidden from the public unless it is visibly zero; an arrow labelled ConvertBack, amount public, out to holder B's public balance. Below: public everywhere, who sends to whom, when and how often, and the total held in confidential form. The issuer reads every confidential balance, as does an auditor if the token names one, and no setting turns this off. A balance is visibly zero when it is new, when its inbox was just merged, or after a clawback.">
   155	  <figcaption>Figure 1. Amounts are hidden inside confidential form and public at its edges. Who pays whom is public everywhere, and the issuer reads every balance.</figcaption>
   156	</figure>
   157	
   158	**Hidden from the public:** each holder's balance, and the amount of each Send.
   159	
   160	**Public, always:**
   161	
   162	- The sender and receiver of every transfer, and when it happened, so how often
   163	  anyone transacts (P-4, P-11).
   164	- Every amount converted in or out, each one separately.
   165	- The token's total supply, and the total held in confidential form.
   166	- That a balance is exactly zero, in three cases, below.
   167	
   168	**Who can read every balance:** the issuer, always. XLS-96 keeps a second copy of
   169	each confidential balance, encrypted to the issuer's key, and no setting turns it
   170	off (P-9). An auditor can read them too, if the token names one, and only one is
   171	supported (E-11). I ran this rather than inferring it. The holder, the issuer and
   172	the auditor each decrypted the same balance, 500, and each read 475 after a
   173	25-unit Send (E-58).
   174	
   175	**Who can spend:** only whoever holds the holder's encryption secret, because a
   176	Send's proof cannot be made without it (E-33). Where that secret is derived from
   177	the account's master seed, as this project derives it, whoever holds the seed holds
   178	the secret too. The issuer cannot spend a holder's balance. If the token allows
   179	clawback, a setting that lets an issuer take tokens back, the issuer can destroy a
   180	confidential balance, crediting no one, and this project's tokens allow clawback
   181	(E-12). Unless the token's flags were made unchangeable when it was created, the
   182	issuer can also turn on locking later and freeze balances. That second power I read
   183	in rippled's source and did not run (E-290).
   184	
   185	<figure>
   186	  <img src="/images/posts/amounts-not-relationships/figure-2-who-can-read-who-can-spend.svg" alt="A table of who can see what. Columns: who pays whom and when; amounts converted in or out; a holder's balance; a Send's amount; can spend a balance. Anyone: yes, yes, only whether it is visibly zero, no, no. A holder: yes, yes, their own, their own, their own with both their keys. The issuer, highlighted: yes, yes, every one, every one, and no, though if the token's settings allow, it can destroy or freeze one. An auditor, if the token names one: yes, yes, every one, every one, no.">
   187	  <figcaption>Figure 2. Who can read what, and who can spend. A dashed cell is a partial yes.</figcaption>
   188	</figure>
   189	
   190	**Zero is sometimes visible.** XLS-96 writes a fixed encryption of zero, which
   191	anyone can recompute from public inputs, in three places: a new confidential
   192	balance, an inbox that a MergeInbox has just emptied, and a position clawed back.
   193	So enrolment is publicly visible. The English documentation said this value could
   194	not be told apart from other ciphertexts. I recomputed it from public inputs and
   195	matched it byte for byte against live Devnet state (F-1, E-59), reported it, and the
   196	English page was corrected. A balance spent down to zero holds a randomised
   197	encryption of zero, and is not recognisable (E-211).
   198	
   199	**The public numbers bound the hidden ones.** If a holder converts in 500, receives
   200	nothing, and converts back 400, anyone can work out that the other 100 is either
   201	still held or has left by confidential Send. No key is needed. I first wrote that
   202	the 100 *"left by transfer"*. That overstated what an observer learns, and it is
   203	recorded as a correction (R-7).
   204	
   205	---
   206	
   207	## No rotation, no recovery
   208	
   209	A registered key can never be changed (E-9). XLS-96 has no key rotation and no key
   210	recovery (P-10). If a holder loses their key, and any seed it could be re-derived
   211	from, the balance cannot be spent. The only remedy is an issuer clawback, which
   212	destroys the balance.
   213	
   214	A draft standard, XLS-99, by Aanchal Malhotra and Yinyi Qian, proposes rotation for
   215	holder, issuer and auditor keys, and recovery from key loss. When I checked, rippled
   216	declared its amendment as not supported, in its development branch and in its
   217	latest release candidate, and Mainnet, Testnet and Devnet did not know it (E-353).
   218	So there is no rotation or recovery in XLS-96, or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet,
   219	today.
   220	
   221	---
   222	
   223	## The example: a confidential receivables facility
   224	
   225	To test the standard against that business case, I built the core of such a
   226	facility.
   227	
   228	The bank issues a token. An ordinary XRPL account, which this project calls the
   229	Dedicated Account, holds the float, the money the facility advances, and converts it
   230	into confidential form once. Suppliers enrol, draw down by confidential Send, and
   231	repay the same way. At the end, what is left of the float is retired in several
   232	parts, called tranches, by ConvertBack. It ran on Devnet in 28 validated facility
   233	transactions, besides setting up the token (E-146).
   234	
   235	<figure>
   236	  <img src="/images/posts/amounts-not-relationships/figure-3-the-facility.svg" alt="The facility's flow. The bank, which issues the token and reads every balance, funds the Dedicated Account with a public payment. The Dedicated Account makes one Convert of the whole float, amount public, so the float is confidential. Drawdowns and repayments are Sends between the float and suppliers A, B and C: amounts hidden from the public, who and when public; each supplier's limit, draws and what it owes are hidden from the public. Each supplier enrols with a small public payment and its own Convert, both amounts public. At the end, what is left of the confidential float is retired in tranches, and each ConvertBack's amount is public. The public totals still bound the hidden amounts.">
   237	  <figcaption>Figure 3. The facility as it ran on Devnet. The amounts that move between the float and the suppliers are hidden; the amounts at the edges are not.</figcaption>
   238	</figure>
   239	
   240	**Anyone can see** the size of the float, because converting it publishes the
   241	amount. They can see which suppliers enrolled, who drew and repaid, on which days,
   242	and how often. And they can see the size of every retirement tranche, because each
   243	ConvertBack publishes its own amount (F-24). My own walkthrough first said a
   244	ConvertBack published only *"the aggregate change"*. The validated transactions
   245	showed each tranche in plaintext.
   246	
   247	**Hidden from the public:** each supplier's limit, the size of each drawdown and
   248	repayment, and what each supplier still owes. The bank, as issuer, sees all of it.
   249	The public totals still bound these amounts, and in a small enough book they can pin
   250	them exactly.
   251	
   252	So it hides how much each supplier draws and owes. It does not hide who borrows,
   253	when, how often, or the size of the whole. An early version of the design claimed
   254	the facility *"shows nothing about which supplier drew how much"* (R-1). Which
   255	supplier drew, and when, is public.
   256	
   257	**Against the business case's questions:**
   258	
   259	1. **What each supplier draws and owes:** hidden from the public, though the public
   260	   totals bound it.
   261	2. **Who draws, and when:** public (P-11). A supplier that moves from monthly to
   262	   weekly drawings shows as short of cash without one amount being known. One
   263	   proposed remedy, the float sending to every supplier on a fixed schedule whether
   264	   or not money moves, has not been shown to work, so I do not offer it as one
   265	   (B-10).
   266	3. **One supplier, another's position:** hidden from it, as from the public. Each
   267	   holder's key decrypts its own balance (E-52).
   268	4. **The bank:** reads every position, always (P-9).
   269	5. **An auditor:** reads every position too, if the token names one, and only one
   270	   is supported (E-11). That is a statement about who can decrypt what, not a claim
   271	   that it meets any regulator's requirements (P-6).
   272	6. **A lost key:** if a supplier loses its key and any seed it could be re-derived
   273	   from, the balance cannot be spent. The only remedy is a clawback, if the token
   274	   allows one, and it destroys the balance (P-10, E-12).
   275	7. **The bank, as issuer:** it cannot spend a supplier's balance. If the token's
   276	   settings allow, it can destroy one or freeze one (E-12, E-290).
   277	
   278	So the business case holds for amounts and fails for relationships. A supplier that
   279	minds being seen to borrow at all, or how often, gets no cover from XLS-96.
   280	
   281	Two limits of that run. First, it read the ledger through a public Devnet node. The
   282	design requires a node on the same machine, and a local Devnet node never finished
   283	syncing on the hardware I had, so I accepted that as a named risk (E-148, E-151).
   284	The run says nothing about that requirement. Second, one test driver played the
   285	bank and every supplier and held every seed. The run shows that these transactions
   286	are well formed and that rippled accepts them. It does not show how custody would
   287	work.
   288	
   289	---
   290	
   291	## Reading the specification, and running it
   292	
   293	Several of the things above I learned only by running them:
   294	
   295	- That three different keys decrypt the same balance, through a change (E-58).
   296	- That the encryption of zero matches a value anyone can recompute (F-1).
   297	- That a balance spent to zero is not recognisable. My own observer page had
   298	  labelled every ciphertext that was not the fixed zero as *"Non-zero"*, and a
   299	  holder whose balance decrypted to 0 disproved it (E-211).
   300	- That a failing transaction is not simply rejected. A `tec` result, one class of
   301	  XRPL failure code, is still applied to the ledger: the fee is charged and the
   302	  account's sequence number is used, though what the transaction asked for does not
   303	  happen. The submission parameter `fail_hard` asks the node to discard it instead.
   304	  I ran both on Devnet with a plain Payment that fails with `tecNO_AUTH`: the same
   305	  signed bytes were applied without the flag, and discarded with it (E-149).
   306	
   307	That last one matters more for confidential transactions than for plain ones,
   308	because a `tec` keeps the transaction's fields, ciphertexts included. If a signer
   309	reads a wrong destination key from a dishonest node, the amount is published
   310	encrypted to that key for good, even though the transaction fails. That case I read
   311	in rippled's source and did not run (F-23).
   312	
   313	Running is not a substitute for reading what others have already found. Several
   314	things I first recorded as findings turned out to be issues that Trail of Bits'
   315	review had already found and Ripple had fixed.
   316	
   317	---
   318	
   319	## What the reviews caught
   320	
   321	Design decisions and fixes went through rounds of adversarial review. These were
   322	the project's own reviews: not outside audits, and not reviews by outside security
   323	professionals. Each round gave its review passes deliberately different material,
   324	so that their agreement would mean more than one reading copied three times. The
   325	repository keeps more than sixty numbered review records, including the ones that
   326	found me wrong. A few of the catches:
   327	
   328	- **A secret not wiped from memory, behind a comment explaining why it could not
   329	  be.** The comment said the secret's type belonged to an outside library. It was
   330	  the project's own type, and one search of its file showed it had no wiping at all
   331	  (E-200).
   332	- **A design claim that four review passes independently ruled unsound.** I had
   333	  written that the project's local read-only web viewer *"moves no trust
   334	  boundary"*. It added no signing authority. But it re-served, to any local user,
   335	  data the project protects with file permissions (E-230). That was the viewer that
   336	  runs on the holder's machine, before the hosted demo existed; the demo serves only
   337	  static files.
   338	- **A release gate that passed a Content Security Policy every browser refused.**
   339	  The gate hashed inline scripts over the file's bytes. Browsers hash the text they
   340	  parse, which differs. Only loading the pages in a real browser showed it (E-334).
   341	- **Fixes that did not fix.** In one review's second round, five of the first
   342	  round's fixes had not discharged their findings. Only the review pass that ran
   343	  each finding's own example against the fixed code found them (E-345).
   344	
   345	The lesson I keep relearning: fixing something and describing the fix are two acts
   346	that fail separately. A review that reads my summary of a finding will tick the
   347	summary.
   348	
   349	---
   350	
   351	## Checks that catch a false sentence
   352	
   353	The working rule is that a claim needs its evidence before it is written. The
   354	claims register holds each established claim with what supports it, and twelve
   355	standing prohibitions, P-1 to P-12, on what may not be claimed at all: that XLS-96
   356	hides identities, that holders are private from the issuer, that it supports key
   357	rotation, any benchmark without its hardware and method, and any claim that a
   358	source does *not* say something without the search that would show otherwise.
   359	
   360	Prose drifts anyway, so some of it is enforced by checks that run in CI. One fails
   361	when a retracted phrase reappears without its correction. One fails when a note
   362	meant for upstream says something is missing from a source and does not record the
   363	search that found it missing. One keeps the register's derived indexes in step with
   364	it.
   365	
   366	They do not catch everything. The register keeps nine correction records, R-1 to
   367	R-9. Most withdraw or narrow something this project claimed; one records a
   368	retraction that was itself reversed. R-8 said every confidential transaction needs
   369	both of a holder's keys, when a MergeInbox needs only the account key; it was on the
   370	public demo until a review pass found it repeated in a diagram caption. R-9 came
   371	from reviewing this post. The README and the demo summarised the facility as hiding
   372	*"the shape of the book, not its size"*, and a reader new to the project took
   373	*shape* to mean who borrows and when, which is public. That sentence is replaced
   374	everywhere, and a check now refuses it.
   375	
   376	At one point the register still listed as open four filings that upstream had
   377	already fixed (E-316). Nothing re-checked them until I surveyed every filing at
   378	source. That survey now runs before anything I publish about them, this post
   379	included.
   380	
   381	---
   382	
   383	## What went upstream
   384	
   385	This project has filed eleven issues in four XRPLF repositories. Their state when I
   386	checked, read at source (E-353):
   387	
   388	- **Four resolved.** Three issues against the XLS-0096 text were resolved in the
   389	  merged standard. The documentation's sentence calling the zero value
   390	  indistinguishable was corrected on the English page. The Japanese translation was
   391	  made from the text before the fix, and still carries it.
   392	- **The mpt-crypto build.** Its lockfile pinned an OpenSSL revision that the
   393	  documented package remote did not serve. Fixed on mpt-crypto's main branch, not
   394	  yet in a release. I re-ran the check against the merged commit, and it resolves.
   395	- **The fixed zero, from JavaScript.** mpt-crypto's WASM and npm packages did not
   396	  expose the function that computes the fixed encryption of zero, which is the check
   397	  an outside observer most needs. A maintainer agreed and a pull request is approved
   398	  and not merged. I have offered to write the JavaScript wrapper once it is
   399	  released.
   400	- **Three filed most recently, against mpt-crypto, with no reply yet:** an
   401	  ambiguity in what the compact sigma paper's nonce input covers; a WASM build
   402	  script that fails outside its pinned toolchain; and a proof-size total in the
   403	  paper that assumes a ciphertext component is sent once, where rippled and XLS-0096
   404	  send it per recipient.
   405	- **A question to XRPL-Standards**, whether a confidential balance is meant to stay
   406	  invisible to the accounting of the ledger's vaults (XLS-65), which pool one asset
   407	  and issue shares against it, has had no reply in nearly two months.
   408	- **A filing to rippled that listed only things done well** was closed without
   409	  comment the day it was filed, so its reason is not known. It also fit neither of
   410	  that repository's two issue templates, and the project's filing rules now forbid a
   411	  positives-only filing to a bug tracker.
   412	
   413	I do not call any of these new, or unreported. Of the three outside reviews of
   414	upstream's code, I could check my findings against one.
   415	
   416	---
   417	
   418	## What it does not show
   419	
   420	- **No run against a local node.** Every Devnet read went to the public cluster
   421	  (E-151).
   422	- **Custody is accepted, not solved.** The issuer can erase or freeze the facility's
   423	  float. The Dedicated Account's key both moves the float and decrypts every amount
   424	  sent to or from it, so those two powers cannot be held apart (E-266).
   425	- **The key derivation is unpublished.** It is specified in this repository only, so
   426	  a holder with their master seed but not this repository cannot reconstruct their
   427	  key. Treat it as lock-in until it is published.
   428	- **A hostile process running as the same user** can read the encryption secret out
   429	  of memory.
   430	
   431	---
   432	
   433	## Try it
   434	
   435	The demo is static pages built from one snapshot of Devnet. It signs nothing and
   436	holds no keys. It shows what an observer reads of four test accounts, including
   437	which balances are visibly zero; which encrypted copies the issuer can read, without
   438	publishing the figures; and what each kind of key can do. It does not show the
   439	facility, whose record is in the repository.
   440	
   441	To transact, you run the signer yourself, on your own machine. The README explains
   442	how to build it and run the local version of the site. It does not yet walk through
   443	creating a holder profile and funded Devnet accounts, which a transaction needs.
   444	
   445	The repository has the Rust signer, the TypeScript facility, the read-only web
   446	viewer, the claims register and the review records, under Apache-2.0.
   447	
   448	---
   449	
   450	## What to take from it
   451	
   452	- **XLS-96 hides amounts, not relationships.** Balances and Send amounts are
   453	  hidden from the public. Who pays whom, when and how often is not. In a
   454	  receivables facility, that protects each supplier's figures, and not the fact or
   455	  the rhythm of its borrowing.
   456	- **The edges are public.** Every Convert and ConvertBack publishes its amount, and
   457	  the totals bound what is hidden.
   458	- **The issuer sees everything.** It reads every balance and, if the token's
   459	  settings allow, can destroy or freeze one.
   460	- **Keys cannot be rotated or recovered**, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet, Testnet or
   461	  Devnet today. XLS-99 is a draft that would add both.
   462	- **Running it found things reading did not**, and reading what others had already
   463	  found saved me from calling their findings mine.
   464	
   465	**Next:** the same study on EVM chains.
   466	
   467	If something in this is wrong, please tell me, by an issue on the repository. The
   468	register has a section for corrections, and it has nine entries.
   469
