    35	
    36	Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on its Devnet test network. But what it hides is narrower than the word suggests: amounts, not relationships.
    37	
    38	XLS-96, the XRP Ledger's standard for confidential transfers, is final. As I write this it is switched on only on Devnet, not on Mainnet or Testnet. I built the core of a receivables facility on it, a bank paying suppliers early against their invoices, and ran it to see exactly what an outside observer can read. That is the business case: how much a supplier draws, and how often, shows its cash position, which a supplier has every reason to keep to itself. I am running the same study on EVM chains; this is the XRP Ledger half, and the EVM results will follow.
    39	
    40	Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each transfer between confidential balances. In the facility, that is each supplier's limit, how much it draws and what it owes.
    41	
    42	Public: who pays whom, when and how often. Every amount moved into or out of confidential form, including the size of the float and of each part of it converted back at the end. And some zero balances, which anyone can recognise. So a supplier that starts drawing weekly instead of monthly is visible to everyone, without one amount being known.
    43	
    44	The token's issuer can read every balance, always, and so can one auditor if the token names one. No setting turns that off. For a regulated issuer that may be the point. For a holder, it is where the privacy ends.
    45	
    46	Keys cannot be rotated or recovered, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet, so key custody has to be right from the first transaction. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.
    47	
    48	Where it could, the project ran its claims on the ledger instead of reading the specification, and it says which ones it only read. It keeps a public register of what it may claim and what it got wrong. It filed eleven issues with the XRPLF repositories on GitHub: five are resolved upstream so far, and the rest are open or were closed without comment. None is claimed as new; upstream's code has had three outside reviews, and I could read only one of their reports.
    49	
    50	It is a research project on a test network: not audited, not production-ready.
    51	
    52	The write-up: https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
    53	A read-only demo: https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app
    54	The code and the claims register: https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions
    55	
    56	XLS-96 is the work of Murat Cenk, Aanchal Malhotra, Ayo Akinyele, Peter Chen, Shawn Xie and Yinyi Qian; its send proof builds on Tess Dore and Murat Cenk's compact sigma protocol.
    57

    47	# X (single long post)
    48	
    49	Can you move tokens confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, on Devnet, under XLS-96. I built the core of a receivables facility on it and ran it to see exactly what it hides. The short answer: amounts, not relationships.
    50	
    51	Hidden from the public: each holder's balance, and the amount of each Send between confidential balances.
    52	
    53	Public: who pays whom, when and how often. Every amount converted into or out of confidential form. And some zero balances: the ledger writes a fixed encryption of zero, which anyone can recompute from public inputs, for a new balance, an inbox just merged and a position clawed back. I matched it byte for byte against live Devnet state.
    54	
    55	The issuer reads every balance, always. XLS-96 keeps a second copy encrypted to the issuer's key, and no setting turns it off. That is by design, and it means "confidential" here is confidentiality from the public. If the token allows clawback, the issuer can also destroy a confidential balance.
    56	
    57	Keys cannot be rotated or recovered, in XLS-96 or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes both.
    58	
    59	In the facility, that means the float, which suppliers drew on which days, and every tranche retired at the end are public. Each supplier's limit, draws and what it owes are not, though the public totals still bound them.
    60	
    61	Eleven issues went upstream to the XRPLF repositories; five are resolved so far. The write-up's claims cite rows of a public claims register, and the register keeps its own corrections.
    62	
    63	I am running the same study on EVM chains. Those results will follow.
    64	
    65	A research project on Devnet: not audited, not production-ready.
    66	
    67	Write-up: https://nandan.me/writing/amounts-not-relationships/
    68	Demo: https://xrpl-confidential-positions.vercel.app

    63	
    64	---
    65	
    66	## Why it matters: the business case
    67	
    68	Large buyers often pay their suppliers' invoices weeks or months after delivery. A
    69	supplier that needs the cash sooner can draw it from a bank against those invoices,
    70	and repay when the buyer pays. That is receivables finance, and its numbers are
    71	sensitive in a specific way:
    72	
    73	- **A supplier's drawings show its cash position.** One that draws more, or more
    74	  often, is short of cash. Published, that tells its competitors, its customers and
    75	  its other lenders.
    76	- **The bank's limits and balances are its book.** What it has lent each supplier,
    77	  and against what limit, is its exposure, and it does not publish that.
    78	- **The suppliers should not see each other.** A supplier that could read another's
    79	  limit and drawings would learn its position and what the bank granted it.
    80	
    81	Why put this on a shared ledger at all? Off one, the same facility lives in several
    82	records, the bank's and each supplier's, which have to be reconciled. The usual case for a
    83	shared ledger is one record that the bank, the suppliers and a supervisor all read,
    84	with the money moving on that record. This post does not test that case. It tests
    85	whether the privacy the business needs survives the move.
    86	
    87	That is the dilemma. On a public ledger in plaintext, every drawing is published, and
    88	with it each supplier's cash position. On a private ledger, much of what a shared
    89	record was for is given up. Confidential transfers are an attempt at the middle:
    90	amounts encrypted on a public ledger, and readable by the parties who answer for the
    91	book.
    92	
    93	So a business would ask concrete questions before using them:
    94	
    95	1. Can the public see what each supplier draws and owes?
    96	2. Can the public see who draws, and when?
    97	3. Can one supplier see another's position?
    98	4. Can the bank see every position? It lends the money, so it must.
    99	5. Can an auditor or supervisor see them too?
   100	6. What happens if someone loses a key?
   101	7. What can the bank do to a supplier's balance without the supplier?
   102	
   103	The facility below answers them as it ran on Devnet.
   104	
   105	---
   106	
   107	## What XLS-96 is, briefly
   108	
   109	The XRP Ledger is public: anyone can read every account and every transaction.
   110	Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its token types: an account issues a
   250	them exactly.
   251	
   252	So it hides how much each supplier draws and owes. It does not hide who borrows,
   253	when, how often, or the size of the whole. An early version of the design claimed
   254	the facility *"shows nothing about which supplier drew how much"* (R-1). Which
   255	supplier drew, and when, is public.
   256	
   257	**Against the business case's questions:**
   258	
   259	1. **What each supplier draws and owes:** hidden from the public, though the public
   260	   totals bound it.
   261	2. **Who draws, and when:** public (P-11). A supplier that moves from monthly to
   262	   weekly drawings shows as short of cash without one amount being known. One
   263	   proposed remedy, the float sending to every supplier on a fixed schedule whether
   264	   or not money moves, has not been shown to work, so I do not offer it as one
   265	   (B-10).
   266	3. **One supplier, another's position:** hidden from it, as from the public. Each
   267	   holder's key decrypts its own balance (E-52).
   268	4. **The bank:** reads every position, always (P-9).
   269	5. **An auditor:** reads every position too, if the token names one, and only one
   270	   is supported (E-11). That is a statement about who can decrypt what, not a claim
   271	   that it meets any regulator's requirements (P-6).
   272	6. **A lost key:** if a supplier loses its key and any seed it could be re-derived
   273	   from, the balance cannot be spent. The only remedy is a clawback, if the token
   274	   allows one, and it destroys the balance (P-10, E-12).
   275	7. **The bank, as issuer:** it cannot spend a supplier's balance. If the token's
   276	   settings allow, it can destroy one or freeze one (E-12, E-290).
   277

    41	
    42	Can a token move confidentially on the XRP Ledger? Yes, under a standard called
    43	XLS-96, and today only on Devnet. A new feature reaches the XRP Ledger as an
    44	amendment, which a network's validators switch on. When I checked on 22 October
    45	2026, XLS-96's amendment, `ConfidentialTransfer`, was enabled on Devnet, and
    46	supported but not enabled on Mainnet and Testnet. That reading goes stale; the
    47	repository has a script that takes a fresh one.
    48	
    49	What XLS-96 hides is narrower than the word *confidential* suggests. It hides
    50	balances, and the amounts of transfers between confidential balances. It does not
   175	**Who can spend:** only whoever holds the holder's encryption secret, because a
   176	Send's proof cannot be made without it (E-33). Where that secret is derived from
   177	the account's master seed, as this project derives it, whoever holds the seed holds
   178	the secret too. The issuer cannot spend a holder's balance. If the token allows
   179	clawback, a setting that lets an issuer take tokens back, the issuer can destroy a
   180	confidential balance, crediting no one, and this project's tokens allow clawback
   181	(E-12). Unless the token's flags were made unchangeable when it was created, the
   182	issuer can also turn on locking later and freeze balances. That second power I read
   183	in rippled's source and did not run (E-290).
   184

   190	**Zero is sometimes visible.** XLS-96 writes a fixed encryption of zero, which
   191	anyone can recompute from public inputs, in three places: a new confidential
   192	balance, an inbox that a MergeInbox has just emptied, and a position clawed back.
   193	So enrolment is publicly visible. The English documentation said this value could
   194	not be told apart from other ciphertexts. I recomputed it from public inputs and

# CLAIMS register

⚠ **`tapFailHard` in this document is THIS PROJECT'S SHORTHAND and appears zero times in rippled** — the real names are `fail_hard` (the RPC parameter) and `TapFailHard` (the internal apply flag). See [`docs/VOCABULARY.md`](docs/VOCABULARY.md). The code always used the real one.

**The register.** Every capability claim in a README, demo, post or conversation gets an entry here with the test result or primary citation that supports it. **Before publishing anything, diff the new claims against this register.**

**Human-gated checklist, not automation.** CI cannot judge whether prose overclaims. Do not add a CI job and call it solved.

|---|---|
| **Navigate** | [`docs/CLAIMS-INDEX.md`](docs/CLAIMS-INDEX.md) — one line per row, generated. ⚠ Do not hand-edit it; `make check-claims-index` fails if it drifts. |
| **Statuses** | `SUPPORTED` evidence attached · `PENDING` asserted, evidence not attached, **may not be published** · `BLOCKED` never claim · `RETRACTED` was claimed, found wrong — **keep the row** |
| **Sections** | [Standing prohibitions](#standing-prohibitions--never-claim) · [Established](#established) · [Pending](#pending--asserted-not-yet-supportable) · [Findings](#findings--verified-file-upstream-before-publishing) · [Retracted](#retracted) |
| **History** | [Revision history](#revision-history) — moved to the end 2026-09-04. ⚠ It was **5,358 characters of unbroken prose above the first heading**, so nothing in this file was visible without scrolling past it. |

## Standing prohibitions — never claim

| # | Claim | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P-1 | That this work makes XRPL quantum-safe or quantum-resistant | It does not |
| P-2 | That an application-layer PQ scheme protects funds at the ledger level | An adversary who breaks secp256k1 signs a valid classical transaction and the network accepts it |
| P-3 | That any amendment is live or enabled, without a dated `feature` RPC check | Amendment state is a reading, not knowledge |
| P-4 | That a Confidential MPT demo hides identities | It hides amounts and balances. Sender and receiver remain public |
| P-5 | That anything here is trustless, non-custodial, decentralised, audited, production-ready or secure | None of it is; ADR-0001 names the trusted parties |
| P-6 | That anything is compliant with regulation in a named jurisdiction | Not a compliance project |
| P-7 | That analysis of published work is original research | Cite Cenk, Malhotra, Akinyele, Chen, Xie, Qian by name where the work is theirs. **Add Tess Dore (2026-08-16):** the compact sigma protocol, the twisted-ElGamal analysis and the Bulletproofs++ analysis are Dore & Cenk, RippleX Research — Dore is *not* an XLS-0096 author and is easy to omit by copying E-1's list |
| P-8 | Any benchmark number without hardware, parameter set and methodology | Includes re-quoting XLS-0096 §14.2's "laptop-class CPU" timings — see B-1 |
| P-9 | That holders are private from the issuer | The issuer's decryption mirror is mandatory. No configuration makes this false |
| P-10 | That XLS-96 supports key rotation or key recovery | It supports neither, at any level |
| P-11 | That confidential transfers hide *who* transacts, or *when*, or *how often* | Only amounts are hidden. The counterparty graph and event timing are fully public |
| P-12 | **Any claim that a source does NOT say something — *nothing documents it*, *no such field*, *not exported*, *nobody has called it out*, *I could not find it* — without the search that would falsify it recorded alongside** | It is an assertion about a whole corpus and one search settles it. **Three graded rows failed this way on 2026-08-26** (E-155, E-156), two of them **positives**: U-15 quoted a sentence XLS-0096 has never contained; U-12 said a property was *"not called out anywhere I found"* when the spec states it **twice**, once in wording identical to the benefit claimed as an original reading. ⚠ **This shape survives review because it does not look like a claim** — a quotation has quotation marks, a benchmark visibly wants a methodology, and *"nobody has documented this"* reads as modesty. Gated by `tools/check-negative-claims.ts` |

## Phase 3 — the two posts

**Gate:** the repository is public and the demo is live, so both posts link to
something a reader can check. Each draft runs `claims-check` and one adversarial read
before it is published, and the owner signs off the final text.

**Ruled 2026-10-21: on the day each post is published, run `compare-deployed`
against the live URL** (`web/hosted/README.md` step 7), after breaking it on a copy
of the output as E-349 did, with a zeroed digest and an altered header. A post
links a demo checked that day, and waits if the comparison fails.

⚠ **Gate amended 2026-10-18, on E-316: every filing is re-surveyed at source before
a word of either post is drafted.** The survey is the one E-316 records: the comments
on each issue this project filed, by anyone but this project; `gh pr view` on every
PR a closing comment names; the fix grepped in the merged text rather than taken from
the comment. Each filing is then described by its outcome on the survey date, not by
its register row. Grep every language copy of a changed page: on 2026-10-20 a fix
had reached the English page and not its Japanese translation (E-341). On 2026-10-18 the register carried four filings as open that
upstream had fixed and closed in September; a post written from it would have called
four fixed defects open. Phase 1's README states the same outcomes in its *Upstream*
section and runs the same survey before publication.

1. **The blog post** (`nandan.me/writing`). The honest spine: what XLS-96 hides
   (amounts and balances), what it does not (who, when, how often — P-4, P-11), that
   the issuer can always decrypt (P-9), that there is no rotation or recovery (P-10)
   in XLS-96 or on Mainnet, Testnet or Devnet, while a draft, XLS-99, proposes both
   (added 2026-10-20, E-341),
   Devnet only with a dated amendment reading (P-3). Then the part that is genuinely
   this project's own: execution over reading, the adversarial rotations and what they
   caught, the gates that catch a false sentence, and the findings filed upstream.
   Credit Cenk, Malhotra, Akinyele, Chen, Xie, Qian and Dore where the work is theirs
   (P-7). **Do not describe the Trail of Bits report as *the* audit of this code**,
   and do not call a finding *unreported* or *new*: B-30 records a second audit,
   the Sherlock XRP Ledger Attackathon, whose findings this project cannot read,
   and B-31 a third, Zellic's scan of mpt-crypto, known only through the three
   identifiers mpt-crypto#147 cites (added 2026-10-18). Name all three, and say
   which one could be checked.
2. **The LinkedIn post.** Short, answers the question in the first line, links the
   demo, the repository and the post. Same prohibitions. No benchmark number without
   hardware and method (P-8). Nothing that reads as *audited*, *production-ready* or
   *secure* (P-5).

Round-one fixes are mostly present, but the LinkedIn outside-review disclosure remains incomplete, the social amendment-status claim relies on an author-only date, and new business-case and lost-key statements exceed the cited evidence. The topic-pages link resolves to a file in this tree, and the id-finding instructions are usable, though the definitions are shorthand rather than complete descriptions of each register section.

Full review comments:

- [P2] Qualify the business-case claims as illustrative — $USER_TMP/T/r064a.hJ99Di/repo/docs/posts/BLOG-2026-10-22-draft.md:73-79
  The new business-case section presents several uncited generalizations as facts: that buyers often pay weeks or months after delivery, that drawing more or more often means a supplier is short of cash, that this information tells competitors, customers and lenders, and that banks do not publish their exposures. The register and cited project materials support the facility example, not these market and business claims. Add sources or frame these as assumptions for the example. The LinkedIn sentence “how much a supplier draws, and how often, shows its cash position” repeats the unsupported inference; “For a regulated issuer that may be the point” also risks implying regulatory expectations the post has not established. (Blog lines 68–79; LinkedIn line 38.)

- [P2] Name the outside reviews in the LinkedIn post — $USER_TMP/T/r064a.hJ99Di/repo/docs/posts/LINKEDIN-2026-10-22-draft.md:48-48
  The post says upstream's code had three outside reviews and that one report was readable, but does not name the reviews or identify which report could be checked. Phase 3 explicitly requires both posts to name Trail of Bits, Sherlock and Zellic and say which one could be checked; the blog's fuller disclosure does not satisfy that requirement for this separate post. Add the names and identify Trail of Bits as the report that could be checked.

- [P2] Date the social posts' Devnet amendment claim — $USER_TMP/T/r064a.hJ99Di/repo/docs/posts/SOCIAL-2026-10-22-draft.md:49-49
  The social copy says the feature is available “on Devnet” (for example, X line 49), but the only date for the amendment reading is in the author-only note. P-3 requires a dated feature-RPC check alongside an amendment-status claim, and a post's timestamp does not establish that the reading is current or travel with copied text. Include the reading date in the post or avoid implying current enabled status.

- [P2] Avoid calling clawback the only lost-key remedy — $USER_TMP/T/r064a.hJ99Di/repo/docs/posts/BLOG-2026-10-22-draft.md:272-274
  The answer says “The only remedy is a clawback” if the token allows one. E-10 supports that losing the ElGamal key permanently loses access, and E-12 says clawback burns the balance; neither establishes that clawback is the only possible remedy. The post's own explanation says the key may be derived from a seed, so first distinguish losing the key from losing every seed it could be re-derived from, then describe clawback as an issuer action that may be available rather than the sole remedy.

- [P2] Carry the freeze condition into the figure alt text — $USER_TMP/T/r064a.hJ99Di/repo/docs/posts/BLOG-2026-10-22-draft.md:186-186
  The visible Figure 2 cell and its SVG description now say freezing depends on token settings, but the blog's alt text only says “if the token's settings allow,” which omits E-290's material condition: the issuer can turn on locking later unless the token's flags were made unchangeable at creation. The nearby prose states this accurately, but the figure's alternative text must not make a different, less precise claim. State the flags condition in the alt text as well.
